name: Brainstorming (traditional)
diamondNote: Mainly Idea Finding, also Problem and Solution Finding
materials: Black markers, sufficient flip-over sheets, tape
purpose:
Because options are said out loud, the key ground rule is hitchhiking: using other people's options as stepping stones to new ones by association. It mustn't slide into a discussion, so the facilitator keeps diverging and converging strictly apart and stresses postponing judgment.

Use it to:
• Generate a range of unusual ideas.
• Purge at the start of a session, before other diverging techniques.
inShort: An open question is written large on the wall. The RG calls out options; the facilitator numbers them and writes them on a flip chart. The facilitator's writing speed caps the pace.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaG or PaP. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Position the RG. A semi-circle around the flip chart for good eye contact.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment. Recap the rules: quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps; agree a target number of options.
Generate. The RG calls out options one at a time (this doubles as the purge). Number and list them. When the flow slows, restate the problem or push for more, or for the wildest idea.
Check on progress. Guard the mindset; ask the PO whether options are heading the right way and are the kind wanted.
Reflect. Target reached? Ask the PO whether they need more, whether the field is covered, and what to explore further. Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. More options (same or another technique), reverge (e.g. Idea Gallery), a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Write each option down exactly and completely as said.
• Write large and legibly.
• Don't assume people know how to brainstorm, even if they say they do.
• Keep everyone involved, the PO included.
• Face the RG; don't turn your back.
• Consider a separate scribe so you can focus on facilitating.
• When fluency drops, ask for three more each, ask for wild options (the "wild card", a light version of Criminal Round), or prompt with "What if we think about options that…?" using anything that fits, e.g. loose SCAMPER words.
variants:
• Brainwriting with Post-its: faster capture and higher fluency, and the Post-its can be moved for reverging (e.g. Spontaneous Clustering, Sequencing).
• With a graphic facilitator: ideas are drawn rather than written, creating a collective visual memory. Needs a separate process facilitator.
• Ping Pong brainstorming (Van Leeuwen & Terhürne, 2010): two people take turns sharing options; if nothing comes, share an association with a previous one.
• Alternate brainstorming (Treffinger & Nassab, 1998): alternate active generation with silent reflection, so people can catch their breath and jot down options to share next round.
background: Alex Osborn (the O in advertising agency BBDO) found meetings between "creatives" and "suits" unproductive. In the 1940s he introduced rules for "organized ideation", later famous as brainstorming, and wrote them up in Applied Imagination (1953). Most people think they know brainstorming, but few run it well, making it the most misunderstood and misapplied creativity technique.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.1, pp. 40-43

name: Brainwriting with Post-its
diamondNote: Mainly Idea Finding, also Problem and Solution Finding
materials: Post-its, black markers, flip-over sheets, tape
purpose:
A silent version of Brainstorming. The writing speed of one scribe no longer limits the flow, and loud participants no longer dominate.

Use it to:
• Get many varied options fast.
• Balance input from extraverts and introverts.
• Speed up follow-up steps, because every option already sits on a movable Post-it.
• Purge (see Session Duties, duty 3).
inShort: The RG writes options in silence, one per Post-it. The facilitator collects them and places them on a flip chart in view of everyone.

stepByStep.text: Focus on the task. Write the PaG or PaP where all can see it. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a wanted solution and answers questions.
Hand out supplies. Post-its and a marker for each person. Ask for short, readable writing.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment. Repeat the rules: quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Explain the technique if new to the group. State the purpose, the steps and a target number of options.
Generate. People write one option per Post-it and hand it over. The facilitator sticks them up quietly, and reads some aloud after about 20. When the flow drops, ask for more.
Check progress. Watch the mindset. Ask the PO if the options go in the right direction.
Reflect near the end. Target reached? Does the PO need more, or a specific area explored? Read the energy of the room.
Decide the next step. More options with another technique, move to reverging (for example Spontaneous Clustering), take a break, or plan actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Readable, short, specific Post-its make hitchhiking possible.
• Never stack Post-its on top of each other.
• A trained group writes silently while background information gets shared.
• Fluency enhancers keep the flow going: ask for three more each, ask for the wildest option, aim to fill the whole sheet, or read the PaP again.
• Light stimuli from flexibility techniques also work, as long as they stay close to the PaP: "How would a vlogger solve this?", a 5W1H prompt, or a "What if..." question.
• Sense if the group needs a prompt at all. Sometimes silence works best.
variants:
• Other names: stick-em-up brainstorming, stick-on brainstorming, silent brainstorming.
• Collective notebook (Haefele, 1962): for large groups. People log thoughts several times a day, then pick the best. Works well digitally.
• Mixed use: often combined with other diverging techniques as the capture method.
background:
Classic Brainstorming hits two limits: the scribe's writing speed, and shouting favours some people over others. Osborn already tested written variants. Post-its made the written version the standard in almost every session.

Key references: Osborn (1953), Isaksen, Dorval & Treffinger (2000).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.2, pp. 44-47

name: Brainwriting 6.3.5
diamondNote: Mainly Idea Finding, also Solution Finding
materials: Worksheets, markers, tape, flat surface for writing
purpose:
A silent brainstorming variant built on "quantity breeds quality" and hitchhiking. The name says it: 6 participants write 3 ideas per 5-minute round, so in 30 minutes you get up to 108 options. Passing the sheets on makes people build on and improve each other's ideas. It's less spontaneous than other techniques, so it suits incremental change best.

Use it to:
• Produce a guaranteed volume of options.
• Encourage hitchhiking.
• Generate options for incremental change.
• Leave room to reflect and incubate.
• Balance input from extraverts and introverts.
inShort: Six people sit around a table and each writes three options on their worksheet. After five minutes, sheets move to the neighbour, who reads what's there and adds three new options inspired by it. After six rounds everyone has their own sheet back.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaP. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Seat the RG and hand out supplies. Everyone sits in a circle at the table with a worksheet and marker. Ask for clear, short writing and have each person write the PaP at the top of their sheet.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.
Generate (includes the purge). Three options per row. After five minutes, pass sheets clockwise; read what's there and add three new options. Repeat until every box is filled.
Check on progress. Guard the mindset and watch fluency.
Reflect. Ask the PO whether options are heading the right way, whether more are needed, and what to explore further. Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. More options, reverge (e.g. Idea Gallery), a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Flex the round length to the RG's fluency: shorter at first, longer later.
• Options should be readable, short and specific so others can build on them.
• It's meant to be silent and introspective, so discourage side conversations.
• Instead of passing sheets, people can move seats, which adds energy.
• Use large worksheets, or flip-over sheets on the wall that people walk between, so space isn't a limit.
• Six, three and five aren't fixed (see Brainwriting XYZ).
• Write options on Post-its stuck to the sheet so they can be moved later, e.g. for Spontaneous Clustering.
• When fluency drops, use the fluency enhancers from Brainwriting with Post-its.
• You can run several problem statements (or variants) at once, one per sheet. Purge on the main statement first.
variants:
• Brainwriting pool (Geschka, 1979): more sheets than people sit in the middle of the table. Everyone works at their own pace and grabs someone else's sheet for inspiration.
• Brainwriting XYZ: same process, but the facilitator sets the number of people (X), ideas per round (Y) and round length (Z).
• Braindrawing 6.3.5: draw the ideas instead of writing them.
background: Developed by Bernd Rohrbach in 1968 and refined by Helmut Schlicksupp (in Geschka, 1978). Horst Geschka (1979) at the Battelle Institute added extra worksheets so people could work at their own pace, calling it the "brainwriting pool". Gryskiewicz (1980) found brainwriting especially useful for incremental-change options.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.3, pp. 48-51

name: Creative Confrontation
diamondNote: Mainly Idea Finding, also Problem and Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, Post-its, black markers, plus whatever the chosen excursion needs
purpose:
New ideas come from chaos, but most people fear chaos. Creative Confrontation builds safe chaos: it leads the RG step by step into domains far from the problem. The forced fit afterwards stretches flexibility.

Use it to:
• Get options beyond the obvious.
• Train flexibility during diverging.
inShort:
Three moves:

1. Purge on the PaP, to empty the obvious ideas.
2. Excursion, make the familiar strange.
3. Forced fit, make the strange familiar.

stepByStep.text: Focus on the task. PaP visible. PO explains, gives an example, answers questions.
Position the group. RG stands around a large sheet. Post-its and markers for all.
Set the divergent mindset. Repeat the three diverging rules.
Purge if not done yet. One option per Post-it, ask for one more when the flow drops.
Prepare to go further. Tell the group the next step goes deeper. Stress hitchhiking.
Run the excursion. Each excursion has four sub-steps: set the mood, explore the domain, harvest options in that domain, close. See the excursion notes below.
Explain the forced fit. Purpose, steps, questions.
Pick one excursion output to start from.
Force fit. Ask what that output suggests for the PaP, or what it makes people think of in relation to the PaP. Capture every option.
Check progress every 15 to 25 options with the PO. Right direction? Another word from the excursion worth exploring?
Reflect near the end. Target reached? Does the field feel covered?
Decide the next step. More options, reverging, a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• The book prefers a tightly structured run: introduce each step formally and give it time.
• Mark the transitions, for example with a relaxing exercise or 30 seconds of quiet.
• This is deep, slow thinking. Do not rush it.
• Build a personal set of excursions where both you and the RG feel safe.
variants: • DIY excursions. Invent your own. Example "colours of the rainbow": a Flower Association around red, green, yellow and blue, then force fit the petals onto the PaP.
background: Emerged in the early 1960s, after Guilford and Osborn. Focus moves from fluency to flexibility ("slow thinking", Kahneman). Koestler (1964): real novelty comes from colliding incompatible frames of thought. Gordon's Synectics (1961) applied this with a fixed analogy sequence. Prince coined "excursions". De Bono called the family "lateral thinking". Von Oech and Aznar list hundreds of variants.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.4, pp. 52-55

name: Excursion: Criminal Round
diamondNote: Idea Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers, Post-its
purpose:
Everyone has a secret wish to do forbidden things. Playing with this inside a safe session frees options people normally keep to themselves.

Use it to:
• Bring energy back into the RG.
• Get options beyond the obvious.
• Remove the pressure to produce "good" ideas.
inShort: During diverging, the RG shares illegal ideas for the PaP. Then the group converts each criminal idea into a positive one.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood. Explain purpose and steps. Repeat the diverging rules: postpone judgment, quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel. Answer questions. Add a relaxing exercise if needed.
Explore. Ask for options that are forbidden, illegal or would put you in jail. If the flow drops, prime a specific crime type: smuggling, fraud, robbery, and so on.
Harvest. Write the criminal options on a separate sheet. Destroy that sheet before leaving. No photos. This keeps the excursion safe.
Close and force fit. Use the criminal options as stimuli for forced fitting (step 7 of Creative Confrontation).

tipsAndTricks:
• News headlines give endless crime inspiration.
• The round gets loud and silly. Bring the group back to a calm mood afterwards. The forced fit helps. A quiet, inward excursion fits well next, such as Take a Walk or Guided Fantasy.
variants:
• Worst idea. Each person writes a stupid, gross or illegal idea. The neighbour writes a tamed version on top. Pass again and build a better idea on the tamed one. Based on Parnes' "from silly to good".
• Problem reversal. Flip the PaP. "How might we make the dishwasher worse?" or swap keywords: "get kids to play outside" becomes "get the outside to play with kids". Force fit the results back.
background: A textbook example of guiding a group through all three waves of Extended Effort, especially the jump from wave 2 to wave 3, "from silly to good" (Parnes et al., 1977). First written up as Criminal Round by Van Leeuwen and Terhürne (1999/2010). Common among Dutch facilitators.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.5, pp. 56-59. This is step 6 of Creative Confrontation.

name: Excursion: Take a Walk
diamondNote: Idea Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers
purpose:
When the RG's heads are full of the problem and worn out from generating options, a break with input from the outside world helps. Walking also energises through movement, fresh air and a change of scene, and gives the mind time to incubate.

Use it to:
• Turn a break into the start of Creative Confrontation.
• Get the group into an exploring mindset.
• Generate options beyond the obvious.
inShort: The RG strolls through a different environment and brings objects or other inspiration back to the room. These become the starting point for options in other domains.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood (6.1). The RG should be steeped in the PaP and drained by the purge. Before the break, explain the purpose and steps; answer questions.
Walk (6.2). Everyone goes for a walk and picks up one or two objects that strike or inspire them, then brings them back.

Explore the inspirations (6.3). The RG sits in a circle around blank sheets and places their objects on them. Ask each person what the object is and why it struck or inspired them. Note object names and inspirations on a flip-over sheet.
Harvest (6.4). Recap the diverging rules, then go through the objects one by one, drawing out inspiration and aspects. Note them on a separate sheet.
Close and move to forced fitting (6.5). Use the listed aspects as stimuli for Creative Confrontation step 7.

tipsAndTricks:
• If objects can't be taken, ask for observations instead.
• If there are too many, have each person briefly explain, then let the PO pick the most interesting ones.
• "Making the familiar strange" works better in an unrelated setting: a supermarket, DIY store, train station, museum.
• Use Flower Association to dig deeper into an inspiration.
• Works alone, in pairs or in small groups.
• See the session duty Break (§4.3.7) for fitting it into a formal break.
variants:
• Other name: physical excursion.
• Photo excursion (Higgins, 1994): Take a Walk combined with Visual Stimulation. People photograph whatever strikes them (objects, people, situations, textures) to use in forced fitting.
• Back to nature (van Engelen, 2010): Take a Walk combined with Direct Analogy. Pairs walk in nature (or a park) and spot two problems nature has solved and how, e.g. how a tree survives winter by shedding its frost-sensitive leaves. The problems needn't relate to the PaP. After about 15 minutes, force-fit nature's solutions to the PaP. Needs an RG experienced at forced fitting.
background: Wallas (1926/1970) named incubation as its own step in the creative process: stepping away from the PaP and thinking about something else. Experienced facilitators build in incubation with gaps of up to two weeks between announcing and running sessions, and with breaks during sessions. Aznar and Bléas (2018) describe turning the break into a literal excursion inside Creative Confrontation.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.6, pp. 60-63. These are the sub-steps of Creative Confrontation step 6, "generate options in the domain of the excursion".

name: Excursion: Hidden Presumptions
diamondNote: Problem Finding and Idea Finding, sometimes Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers, Post-its
purpose:
Habits and presumptions help us survive, but they pass unnoticed and limit creative thinking. Naming them on purpose and then breaking them opens new options and perspectives.

Use it to:
• Get options beyond the obvious.
• Gain insight into the problem and the solution space.
• Lift thinking constraints from the RG.
• Shape or sharpen the problem statement.
inShort: Use the purge output to expose the built-in presumptions. Break them deliberately in a new diverging round.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood. Purpose, steps, diverging rules, questions, a relaxing exercise if needed.
Explore. Put the first ten purge options on a separate sheet. Ask what they have in common, what all of them assume.
Harvest. List every presumption on its own flip-over sheet.
Close and force fit. Use the presumptions as stimuli. Ask for options without presumption 1. When the flow drops, remove presumption 2, then 3.

tipsAndTricks:
• If the first ten options give weak presumptions, repeat with the next ten.
• You can also run it on key words of the PaP: "Which assumption does this word carry?"
• Especially useful in the Problem Finding diamond.
• Instead of removing a presumption, reverse it.
variants:
• Other names: challenging all conventions, assumption smashing, assumption busting, drop an assumption, challenge the rules.
• Design method (visual): everyone sketches a solution. Find what all sketches share. Sketch again without it. Repeat.
• Boundary examination: a mix of Hidden Presumptions and Morphological Synthesis. Highlight the keywords of the PaG, use them as matrix parameters, and list alternatives per keyword.
• Assumption reversal: reverse rather than drop each presumption (Grossman, Rogers & Moore, 1988).
background: Schein (1991) describes three levels of what we see: artefacts, values and norms, and basic assumptions. A chair is an artefact, but we mostly see its function and our belief about it. Naming these frozen beliefs lets us unfreeze them. Described as "Presuppositions" by Van Leeuwen and Terhürne (2010).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.7, pp. 64-67. Step 6 of Creative Confrontation.

name: Excursion: Absurd Questioning
diamondNote: Idea Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers
purpose:
Step-by-step, so it feels safe, yet it produces strong, strange stimuli for forced fitting. Easy, fast and light. A good first verbal excursion for an inexperienced RG.

Use it to:
• Get options beyond the obvious.
inShort: Transform the PaP step by step into absurd territory with a three-stage word matrix. The RG answers the absurd question, then force fits those answers back to the real PaP.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood. Purpose, steps, diverging rules, questions, an exercise if needed.
Build the matrix. Write the PaP. Pick three terms from it as columns. For each term, list substitutes in three stages: nearby, more creative, absurd.
Create the absurd question. Pick one term from each column at random, ideally some from the absurd row. The three form a new question.
Harvest. The RG generates answers to the absurd question on a flip-over sheet.
Close and force fit. Use those answers as stimuli for the real PaP.

tipsAndTricks:
• You can force fit at any point, even from single matrix words.
• If three terms feel too complex, use two. Literature calls this semantic shift or word dance.
• Energy matters. Run an energizer first if needed.
variants: • Provocative sub-division: take one essential PaP term, split it into two concepts, split those again. Combine two words from the tree as stimuli.
background: Inexperienced RGs feel trapped by a strong PaP and stay in the obvious. Humour breaks dominant paradigms. Koestler (1964) saw humour as the archetype of "bisociation". Tassoul (2009) formatted this technique.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.8, pp. 68-71. Step 6 of Creative Confrontation.

name: Excursion: Random Words
diamondNote: Mainly Idea Finding, also Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers, dice or a random word generator
purpose:
Give the RG triggers for new options through words with no obvious link to the problem. A quick excursion.

Use it to:
• Get options beyond the obvious.
• Run a short excursion.
inShort: Show the RG a random word. Either analyse it first, then force fit, or force fit straight from the word.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood. Purpose, steps, diverging rules, questions, an exercise if needed.
Explore. Pick a word at random from a dictionary, or roll dice on the word list.
Harvest (optional). Analyse the word with a Flower Association, or list links between the word and the PaP on the Creative Confrontation worksheet.
Close and force fit.

tipsAndTricks:
• In step 8 of Creative Confrontation you pick one excursion output to build on. Use the word itself, or a petal from its Flower Association.
• The gap from the previous round can feel huge. Your confidence creates the safety.
• A fixed word list and dice give a sense of control. Two dice: one picks the column, one the row.
• The book prints a 6 x 6 word list for dice use (see source page 75).
variants: • Simplified MATEC: pick two random words. Ask the RG how they connect, aiming for at least five links. Pick one link and force fit. See MATEC.
background: Introduced by De Bono (1971). Widely used (Byttebier & Vullings, 2007). Good description in Tassoul (2009).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.9, pp. 72-75. Step 6 of Creative Confrontation.

name: Excursion: Random Objects
diamondNote: Mainly Idea Finding, also Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers, Post-its, markers
purpose:
Most fluency techniques and the earlier excursions work with words. Words are a strong source of inspiration (Alter et al., 1973; Gonçalves et al., 2014), but the brain can also think in pictures and images. Random Objects is an easy way to use that non-verbal capacity.

Use it to:
• Use the RG's non-verbal thinking.
• Generate options beyond the obvious.
inShort: The core is getting inspired by looking at objects, in several possible variations. When the facilitator supplies the objects it's Random Objects (or Random Stimuli). When participants bring them in themselves, it's Take a Walk.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood (6.1). Explain purpose and steps, recap the diverging rules, give everyone paper and a pen, answer questions. Add a relaxing exercise if needed.

Explore the objects (6.2). Seat everyone around a table with 5 to 10 objects. They look at each in turn and let their minds wander, then each picks a favourite. Prompt them to observe it closely and notice their impressions and reactions.
Harvest (6.3). Each person notes their observations, impressions and reactions. Share the interesting ones in plenary and write them on a flip-over sheet.
Close and move to forced fitting (6.4). Use the list of interesting observations as stimuli for Creative Confrontation step 7.

tipsAndTricks:
• Curate your own colourful, appealing set: an apple, a rubber duck, a small instrument, a hat.
• Objects that don't fit the context work best.
• Pairs help people new to the technique.
• Encourage people to play with their object.
• You can skip 6.3 and go straight to forced fitting after the close look.
• Or replace 6.3 with the Creative Confrontation worksheet from the website.
variants:
• Random stimuli: anything can be a stimulus (words, pictures, objects, sounds), hence the broader name.
• Random objects as homework: ask everyone to bring something unexpected from home, e.g. a child's toy, or whatever catches their eye as they look around.
background: It's hard to say who first used objects to spark ideas. Osborn's Applied Imagination (1953) mentions it briefly. Isaksen et al. (2000) describe it as a basic forced-fitting technique, which this book calls Creative Confrontation.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.10, pp. 76-79. These are the sub-steps of Creative Confrontation step 6, "generate options in the domain of the excursion".

name: Excursion: Visual Stimulation
diamondNote: Mainly Idea Finding, also Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers, sharp printed pictures, plain A4 paper
purpose:
A more introvert excursion. Pictures send people on a virtual trip in their heads. Their observations get force fitted to the PaP.

Use it to:
• Tap the non-verbal side of the RG, in a quiet way.
• Get options beyond the obvious.
inShort: Images "make the familiar strange". By analysing pictures, the RG finds new domains and options in those domains.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood. Purpose, steps, diverging rules, questions. Hand out the worksheet and a pen. Show one or two relaxing pictures (landscape, beach, pool with palm trees) to clear minds.
Explore. RG sits around a table with 10 to 20 pictures. Each person picks the one they like most and studies it. Ask what they observe, and what impressions or reactions the picture triggers.
Harvest. Everyone notes observations alone, then shares the interesting ones in plenary. Capture them on a flip-over sheet.
Close and force fit. Use the interesting observations as stimuli.

tipsAndTricks:
• Build your own set: colourful, detailed, sharply printed pictures.
• People get attached to beautiful pictures and want to keep them. Bring spare copies.
• Unusual pictures work best. Mix categories: food, sport, nature, people, technology.
• Pairs help newcomers.
• Mind image rights. Use your own photos or free placeholder sources.
• The worksheet can replace the plenary harvest.
variants: • Visually Identifying Relationships (VIR): the whole RG works with the same three or four pictures and each lists observations and reactions (Isaksen et al., 2000). See also Visuelle Synektik (Alter et al., 1973).
background: From the Battelle research institute in the early 1970s. Pictures proved the richest and safest triggers. Smell, music, taste and texture provoke wider reactions, including fear and blocks. Published in English by Geschka et al. (1976) as Visual Confrontation.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.11, pp. 80-83. Step 6 of Creative Confrontation.

name: Excursion: Guided Fantasy
diamondNote: Mainly Idea Finding, also Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers, plain paper (A4)
website: Video "the windows of your childhood" and the apple-and-worm exercise
purpose:
Generates options beyond the obvious by putting the RG in a quiet, inward mode of thinking in mental images. Keywords for the journey can come from a first analysis of the PaP. Unlike Random Words or Visual Stimulation, the journey isn't meant to lead somewhere unrelated to the PaP; it often heads towards an ideal situation or future.

Use it to:
• Use the RG's non-verbal thinking.
• Generate options beyond the obvious.
• Put the RG in a calm, deep-thinking state.
inShort: The RG goes on a mental journey and makes observations in different domains. They then draw what they saw on a sheet, and those pictures or posters are force-fitted to the PaP. It's a quick, elegant way to capture rich mental imagery.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood (6.1). Explain purpose and steps, recap the diverging rules, answer questions. Start with a short exercise so the RG feels how vivid mental images can be.

Explore (6.2). Seat the RG comfortably in a quiet space and start with a short relaxation. When they're at ease, ask them to close their eyes. In a calm, clear voice, explain how they'll travel: on foot, by a magic helicopter that can go anywhere and through time, or something else that fits. Guide them to each planned stop and ask what they see and feel there. Finish the journey and bring them back to the here and now.
Harvest (6.3). People note observations on Post-its during the journey, or draw sketches or posters afterwards. Debrief by having each person present their images.
Close (6.4). Use the notes, sketches or posters as stimuli for forced fitting (step 7), or as direct input for Solution Finding.

tipsAndTricks:
• Record yourself guiding the journey and practise until your voice is calm and precise.
• Close your own eyes and follow the journey as you narrate.
• Don't have people lie fully down (floor, mattress): they'll relax too deeply or fall asleep.
• It's purely about images. In the debrief, never let people speculate on why someone saw what they saw.
• If observations were captured as notes, follow with a reverging step.
• For a shared vision, compare all the pictures for common elements and striking differences, then explore the differences.
• Because it needs a very different mindset, start with a warm-up showing how easily detailed images come to mind. Example ("the windows of your childhood"): relax and close eyes; picture the house you lived in at twelve and count its windows (90–120 seconds); come back; debrief. The website has a longer apple-and-worm exercise.
variants:
• Other names: Imagery trek (Isaksen et al., 2000), Guided imagery.
• Future Perfect (McWhinney et al., 1997): after building an ideal future vision with Guided Fantasy, make up stories of how that future was reached. See also Tassoul (2009).
background: Gordon (1961) and Prince (1970) described techniques where the RG builds scenarios through mental journeys. Csikszentmihalyi (1997) later called the resulting state "flow". McKim (1972) first set out principles of what he called Visual Thinking. Isaksen et al. (2000) describe it formally as Imagery Trek, and Bromberger (2004) wrote a Dutch book on it.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.12, pp. 84-87. The facilitator prepares the journey's content before the session, or with the RG during the first diamond. These are the sub-steps of Creative Confrontation step 6.

name: Excursion: Personal Analogy
diamondNote: Problem Finding and Idea Finding, sometimes Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers
purpose:
Draws on the RG's empathy and their ability to enter a self-made fantasy (see Guided Fantasy) to understand the PaG more deeply. Especially useful in the first diamond, Problem Finding.

Use it to:
• Use the RG's non-verbal thinking.
• Understand the physical elements of the PaG deeply.
• Generate options beyond the obvious.
inShort: RG members identify with the problem by imagining they are it, or a part of it, and then explore what they feel as that object. It works especially well on technical problems, but there's no reason it can't work on people problems too.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood (6.1). Explain purpose and steps, recap the diverging rules, answer questions. If needed, warm up with a relaxing or image-thinking exercise like "the windows of your childhood" (see Guided Fantasy).

Explore (6.2). Stand the RG in front of a sheet with the problem statement and replace its nouns with "I" or "me". Then probe: "Imagine I am [the object or subject]. How do I feel?" and "If [the object] could talk, what would it say?"
Harvest (6.3). List the feelings, emotions and frustrations the RG voices on a flip chart.
Close (6.4). Move to another analogy or straight to step 7, forced fitting, using the listed feelings as stimuli.

tipsAndTricks:
• Make sure everything is captured in a durable form (Post-its, flip-over sheets, worksheets) for the later stages.
• Drawing the situation helps people empathise.
• Encourage people to give the objects emotions.
• More prompts, all starting "Imagine I am the [object]…": what would I do, say, think, feel? How would I respond? What would annoy me or please me? Who'd be my friend or enemy? What's my favourite part of the day, and which part would I skip?
variants: • Role-play or Bodystorming: go further by having the RG act out the problem, with the lead roles played by subjects from the problem statement.
background: Gordon (1961) brought analogies into deliberate creativity. Synectics describes five stages of excursions built on analogy and metaphor, starting with Personal Analogy as the way to get familiar with the problem. Prince (1970) gave another description. In Japan, Nakayama independently developed the similar NM-method (Schwarz-Geschka, 2010). Most later authors follow Gordon (e.g. Nolan, 1989), sometimes in a different order.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.13, pp. 88-91. These are the sub-steps of Creative Confrontation step 6.

name: Excursion: Direct Analogy or Metaphor
diamondNote: Mainly Idea Finding, sometimes Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers
purpose:
Weisberg (2006) argues that truly new solutions come from fusing insights across domains through metaphor. Harari (2011) credits humans' ability to imagine and live in a dual reality for our success as a species. That makes analogy and metaphor a powerful source of new ideas.

Use it to:
• Reach deeper layers of the RG's knowledge and imagination.
• Generate options beyond the obvious.
inShort: The RG comes up with situations in other fields that share the essence of the PaP. For a selling problem, ask how politicians, religions or fast-food chains sell. Studying how the other field solves it gives inspiration for the PaP.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood (6.1). Explain purpose and steps, recap the diverging rules, answer questions. Add a relaxing exercise if needed.

Find an analogy (6.2). Ask what comparable problems in other fields this reminds people of, whether there's an analogy in biology, or one in the weather. Choose one the RG knows well, so it's a rich source.
Explore it (6.3). Ask how the problem is solved there and how that field approached it. Encourage speculation and fantasy.
Harvest (6.4). List every "solution" from the analogy on a flip chart.
Close (6.5). Move on to another analogy, or go to step 7 and use the listed solutions as forced-fitting stimuli.

tipsAndTricks:
• Pin down the essence of the PaP before hunting for analogies.
• Invite an expert in the chosen domain. Deep knowledge there makes the stimuli much richer.
• Prepare a few fitting metaphors in advance.
• For biology, use www.asknature.org.
• Analogies can get exotic, so the RG has to trust you. Guard the divergent mindset firmly.
• The analogy doesn't need to be "correct" as long as it opens new mental territory.
• Generating analogies and then applying them is tiring, so schedule regular breaks.
• If the analogies stay too close to the PaP, warm up with more imaginative ones first (Personal or Symbolic and Fantasy).
variants:
• Biomimicry / biomimetics (Benyus, 1997): take the analogy straight from patterns and strategies in nature, which has already solved many of our problems. Example: architects studied how African termite mounds keep a near-constant temperature and humidity while outside temperatures swing from 1 to 40 °C. More on the website.
• Attribute Analogy Chains (Koberg & Bagnall, 1974): Morphological Synthesis plus Direct Analogy. List all attributes of the problem or subject, generate analogies for each, then pick one and force-fit.
background: Gordon (1961) and Prince (1970) brought direct analogies into deliberate creativity and found biological metaphors especially strong. That idea grew into the whole field of biomimicry (e.g. Benyus, 1997). More on Synectics on the website.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.14, pp. 92-95. These are the sub-steps of Creative Confrontation step 6.

name: Excursion: Symbolic and Fantasy Analogy
diamondNote: Idea Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers
purpose:
Builds on Personal and Direct Analogy by stretching the RG's metaphorical thinking into poetic and fantastical territory, to get more options beyond the obvious.

Use it to:
• Reach the deeper preconscious and unconscious reserves of the RG.
• Generate options beyond the obvious.
inShort: A further step in "making the familiar strange" that feeds the RG's ability to speculate. Symbolic Analogy draws on art: paintings, films, novels, poetry. Fantasy Analogy goes into a world where wishes come true and the impossible is possible.

stepByStep.text: Set the mood (6.1). Explain purpose and steps, recap the diverging rules, answer questions. Add a relaxing exercise if needed.

Find an analogy (6.2). Symbolic: which artwork, book, film, line of poetry or Bible quote comes to mind when you think of our problem? Fantasy: in our wildest fantasy, how would [the core of the PaP] work? Which fantasy figure comes to mind? How would it behave on Mars? Note all analogies and pick one the RG finds inspiring and knows well.
Explore it (6.3). How is the problem solved there? How could it be? Encourage speculation and fantasy.
Harvest (6.4). List every "solution" from the analogy on a flip chart.
Close (6.5). Move to another analogy, or go to step 7 and use the solutions as forced-fitting stimuli.

tipsAndTricks:
• Find the essence of the PaP first; the Book Title variant helps.
• Analogies get exotic, so trust in the facilitator is crucial. Experience matters, and starting with an easy variant like Superhero builds a less experienced RG's confidence.
• Generating analogies and then applying them is tiring, so take regular breaks.
variants:
• Book title (Gordon, 1972), also "compressed conflict": capture the paradox at the core of the PaP in two seemingly opposite words, usually adjective plus noun ("overwhelming silence", "safe danger").
• Poetic stimulation (Van Leeuwen & Terhürne, 2010): explain limericks or haiku, have everyone write one on the core of the PaP, then read each aloud and force-fit it to the PaP.
• Superhero (Byttebier & Vullings, 2007): pick an extraordinary figure who could tackle the problem (Gandhi, Batman, Mother Teresa, Lara Croft, Philippe Starck) and ask how they'd solve it. Von Oech (1983) adds: which constraints would they ignore, and what expertise would they bring?
background: Gordon (1961) introduced symbolic and fantasy analogies to deliberate creativity. Later variants include Book Title (Prince, 1970), Poetic Stimulation (Van Leeuwen & Terhürne, 2010) and Superhero (Byttebier & Vullings, 2007).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.15, pp. 96-99. These are the sub-steps of Creative Confrontation step 6.

name: Flower Association
diamondNote: Problem Finding and Idea Finding
typeOfProblem: Single and complex (any type of problem)
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers
purpose:
A first look at the context of the PaG or PaP through one or more key elements of the problem statement. Naming associations helps the RG take a first step away from the most obvious directions.

Use it to:
• Loosen the RG up.
• Get into a diverging mindset.
• Get an overview of the solution space.
• Create some distance from the subject.
inShort: Put a word, symbol or sketch for an important aspect of the problem in the centre of a sheet. Everything that comes to mind gets written around it like petals. You often make several flowers for different key elements.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaG or PaP. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Position the RG and hand out supplies. Stand around a large sheet on the wall. Everyone gets Post-its and a marker; ask for clear, short writing.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge (if not done yet). Everyone writes whatever comes to mind, one per Post-it. When it slows (after 5 to 10 minutes), ask for one more each.
Explain the technique. Purpose and steps; answer questions.
Pick a key term. Usually a key element of the problem statement. Write it in the centre and circle it as the heart of the flower.
Generate. Ask what X makes people think of, what it reminds them of, and what it's made up of. Write every word as a petal. When it slows, push for a few more.
Check on progress. Guard the divergent mindset.
Reflect. Ask the PO whether there's another key word worth exploring. Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. Another diverging technique, refine or restate the problem with the new insights (e.g. Restating the Problem), a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Also a great way to get the RG into the divergent mindset.
• Make it more analytical by asking about functions ("What does this object or service do?").
• Pushing for a few more words when fluency drops moves people from clichés to surprising associations.
• Keep every flower on the wall; the words can be stimuli later in the session.
• The RG can write instead of the facilitator: put the sheet on a table and stand around it.
variants:
Other uses:
• As a warm-up or energizer.
• To find interesting discussion topics.
• To explore an abstract or ambiguous term in the PaG or PaP.
• As a start for Random Words: pick a dictionary word at random as the centre, then force-fit one of its petals.

Related techniques:
• Lotus Blossom / MY method (Matsumura Yasuo): more structured and more often used for idea generation. Generate 8 related words around a key word, then use each as a new centre.
• Mind Mapping: similar, also based on free association.
• Chain association: for wider, more creative options, each association triggers the next (water, fish, chips, smartphone, battery), moving further from the start word each time.
background: Association means one word triggers another. Aristotle already named five mechanisms (Vanosmael & De Bruyn, 1989): polar opposites (black/white), parts and wholes (finger/hand), closeness (pen/paper), cause and effect (snow/slippery), and analogy by shape or sound (duck/swan, bike/hike). The name comes from the associations radiating out like petals. The more structured Lotus Blossom was invented by Yasuo Matsumura, director of Clover Management Research in Japan, to bring structure to mind mapping (Tatsuno, 1990).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.16, pp. 100-103

name: How To's or H2's
diamondNote: Problem Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, tape, black marker, large Post-its and a marker for each participant
purpose:
Explores the problem space by producing as many rewordings of the PaG as possible. Using association and the diverging ground rules, the RG finds lots of different angles on the PaG.

Use it to:
• Explore different viewpoints on the PaG.
• Test how accurate the PaG is.
inShort: Works like Brainwriting with Post-its. RG members write as many H2s as they can, one per Post-it. The facilitator collects them and puts them on a flip chart until the target number is reached.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaG. Explore it by asking the PO questions about the task, and let the PO answer the RG's questions.
Hand out supplies. Post-its and a marker each; ask for clear, short writing.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge (if not done yet). Everyone writes whatever comes to mind, one per Post-it. When it slows (5 to 10 minutes), ask for one more, then move on.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps; set a target number.
Generate H2s. Everyone writes their understanding of the PaG as "How to…" statements, one per Post-it, and hands them to the facilitator, who sticks them on the flip chart. Push for more when needed.
Check on progress. Guard the mindset; ask the PO whether the H2s are heading the right way and are the kind wanted.
Reflect. Target reached? Ask the PO whether more are needed and whether they cover the field. Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. More H2s with another technique (e.g. SCAMPER or Personal Analogy), reverge (e.g. Spontaneous Clustering) then converge (e.g. Restating the Problem), a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Purge on the PaG first to clear heads.
• The aim here is good entry points for the second diamond, not the "right" problem.
• Shift viewpoints for richer H2s: "How would X phrase this?", where X is a Who from 5W1H or any relevant actor.
• Mixing in other techniques makes H2s more exciting: SCAMPER ("What if we could substitute…?"), Fantasy Analogy ("How would Superman phrase it?"), Wishful thinking ("What if… weren't an issue?").
• Halfway through, ask the PO to pick two or three H2s that are getting close to the heart of the problem.
variants:
• Other names: redefining, reformulating, reframing, reboxing.
• KJ method (Kawakita, 1977), Japanese: write H2s on cards, then reverge by clustering and converge by restating. The facilitator shuffles the cards and deals a pile to everyone, then reads one H2 aloud; everyone shares similar ones from their pile, forming a set. Each set gets an overarching H2; those are clustered again under higher-level H2s until one H2 remains.
background: A strong starting point for the second diamond is vital for complex open problems, which technical and social problems often are (more than advertising problems). Prince (1970) and his successor Nolan (1989) gave the first explicit description of moving from PaG to PaP. The phrasing comes from the Buffalo CPS school (Parnes, 1997; Isaksen et al., 2000), with its stems "How to…", "Wouldn't it be nice if…" and "In what ways might I…". Now found in almost every modern source (e.g. Tassoul, 2009).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.17, pp. 104-107

name: Interactive Brainsketching
diamondNote: Mainly Solution Finding, sometimes Idea Finding
typeOfProblem: Single (very suitable for design, technical or system problems)
materials: A5-sized Post-its (or plain A4/A3 paper), markers, flip chart, masking tape
purpose:
Sketching helps a lot in shaping and improving ideas, which makes this strong in the third diamond. With groups who sketch naturally, like design students, it also works in the second diamond as an alternative to Brainwriting 6.3.5.

Use it to:
• Develop options in the third diamond.
• Capture thoughts that can't be put into words yet.
• Add chosen options to the group's shared visual memory.
inShort: Each RG member picks their favourite, most exciting or most feasible options from the previous diamond, depending on the PO's direction. They sketch as many ideas from those as they can, one per sheet or large Post-it. After five minutes the sketches move to the next person, who builds on them or draws new ones.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Point to the PaP on the wall. Seat the RG around a large table with room to draw.
Hand out supplies. Large Post-its and markers for everyone.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge (if not done yet). One option per Post-it; when it slows (5 to 10 minutes), ask for one more.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.
Pick converged options. Each person picks a few they're excited about (check with the PO if needed).
Sketch. One option per sheet. After five minutes, pass sketches to the right. The receiver improves them with additions or notes, or draws something new. Repeat until time or energy runs out.
Check on progress. Guard the mindset, especially hitchhiking; ask the PO whether options are heading the right way.
Reflect. Ask the PO whether more are needed and what to explore further. Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. Hang the drawings and reverge (e.g. Idea Gallery or Elevator Pitch), generate more, take a break, or set actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Prepare people for drawing, e.g. with a drawing energizer, and reassure them that what they draw matters more than how well.
• Ask for a catchy title on each sketch; it helps people find and communicate the essence.
• Sketching can slow fluency, especially if people try to make it pretty. Be ready to push the pace.
• If someone's stuck, have them draw several variants of the same option; that often opens a new line of thought.
• Use dark markers so drawings are visible.
• A4 cramps designers; A3 works better for them.
• People can sketch in pairs to build consensus.
• Consider a short pitch of each sketch before passing it on.
variants:
• Third diamond Brainwriting with Post-its: the written version. High-fluency options vary wildly in abstraction, from actionable ideas to single words. Have people (alone or in pairs) pick a few exciting converged options and write more detailed versions, one per Post-it, with several alternatives each.
• Brainstorming with graphic facilitator (Lakin, 1988): a hired graphic facilitator sketches the options, building a shared visual memory. The catch is that a sketch interprets, so the facilitator steers content more than in traditional brainstorming. More common in consensus-building (e.g. change management) than in iCPS.
• Brainstorming with sketches added (van der Lugt, 2001): the facilitator writes options on a flip chart while the RG adds a sketch on individual Post-its. Suits the second diamond.
background: Developed by Pickens (1980) and described by VanGundy (1988, 2005). Remko van der Lugt (2001) compared Brainwriting with Post-its with several brain-drawing variants, originally as a visual alternative for TU Delft design students in the second diamond. Sketching produced fewer options but more hitchhiking, and proved powerful in the third diamond.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.18, pp. 108-111. Starting point: converged options from the second diamond (Idea Finding).

name: Ladder of Abstraction
diamondNote: Mainly Problem Finding, sometimes Idea Finding
typeOfProblem: Complex (especially to nail down the essence)
materials: Flip chart and markers
purpose:
Explores the problem and solution space at different levels of abstraction, a means-end hierarchy. "Why?" makes the statement more abstract and general; "How?" makes it more concrete and specific. The aim is to reframe the problem around its essence and open up the solution space.

Use it to:
• Open up a very narrow solution space to make room for new ideas.
• Focus a very broad, abstract solution space.
• Choose the right level of abstraction for the task.
• Learn a lot about the context of the problem statement.
inShort: Start from the PaG and ask "Why?". Rephrase the answer as a new problem statement and keep asking until you reach the right level. Then go back to the PaG and ask "How?" to get narrower statements. "Why else?" and "How else?" explore sideways at a given level.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaG. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Hand out supplies. Post-its and a marker each; ask for legible writing.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge (if not done yet). One option per Post-it; when it slows (5 to 10 minutes), ask for one more.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.

Climb with "Why?" Put the PaG in the centre of a flip-over sheet. Ask why it matters, why we need a solution, what resolving it would achieve. Turn each answer into a new "How to…", place it above, and link it with an upward arrow. Repeat until it gets too abstract; use "Why else?" to widen a level.

Descend with "How?" Back at the PaG, ask how we could resolve or achieve it. Phrase each answer as a "How to…?" below, with a downward arrow. Repeat until it's too far from the PaG; use "How else?" to widen a level.
Check on progress. Guard the mindset; ask the PO whether options are heading the right way.
Reflect. Ask the PO whether the field is covered and what to explore further. Sense readiness and energy.

Next step. Reverge (e.g. the PO presents the ladder and sums up the insights), converge on key aspects (e.g. Hits or Dots, then Restating the Problem), explore one direction further, take a break, or set actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• You can capture the raw answer first, then stick a rephrased H2 Post-it over it.
• You can start from a generated idea or solution (e.g. from the purge) instead of the PaG; let the PO choose which.
• Very powerful during the intake with the PO before the session.
variants:
• Squeeze and stretch (Koberg & Bagnall, 1974): "Why?" squeezes the problem; "What is… about?" stretches it.
• Why? What's stopping you? (Isaksen et al., 2000): pair "Why?" with "What's stopping you from doing or achieving this now?"
• 5 Why: credited to Sakichi Toyoda and built into the Toyota Production System by Taiichi Ohno, mainly for technical problems. Ask "why?" five times to reach the root cause. In Toyota's example a welding robot stops; five whys later the cause turns out to be a pump with no filter (Toyota Traditions, 2006).
background: Korzybski (1933) created the "Structural Differential" diagram for abstracting; Hayakawa (1979) used an abstraction ladder to explain it. Parnes (1981) used a "Why method" to generate increasingly abstract problem statements. Isaksen, Dorval and Treffinger (2000) described the Ladder of Abstraction with why and how questions as a generating tool for every diverging stage of CPS. Also called the means-end hierarchy or Progressive Abstraction.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.19, pp. 112-115

name: Making a Collage
diamondNote: Any (this description focuses on Problem Finding)
materials: Magazines, scissors, glue, A3 paper, masking tape, black and coloured markers
purpose:
Gluing fragments of found images onto paper to portray a problem, idea or phenomenon. It appeals to intuition and builds an attitude of letting go, taking time, wandering and reflecting. Arranging images reveals new connections and can produce a holistic view of the problem or solution space.

Use it to:
• Get a holistic view of the problem and/or solution space.
• Give the RG quiet time to think about the problem.
• Stretch rational thinking into expansive, intuitive thinking.
• Think about topics that are hard to put into words.
inShort: Participants browse magazines and collect images that somehow appeal to them in relation to the problem. Then each person makes a collage without a preconceived idea (maybe with a theme or vision). Usually something meaningful emerges: a story, a better grasp of the problem, or a direction for solutions.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaG or PaP. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Seat the RG and hand out supplies. Around a large table with magazines, scissors, glue, markers, A3 paper and tape.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge (if not done yet). One option per Post-it; when it slows (5 to 10 minutes), ask for one more.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.

Make collages. Everyone browses and collects appealing images, with no need to justify choices. After 5 to 10 minutes, start composing: combine, arrange, move pieces around until something meaningful emerges. Allow at least 15 minutes and give a five-minute warning.
Title and reflect. Each person titles their collage and writes any ideas or insights on Post-its.
Check on progress. Guard the divergent mindset.
Reflect. Ask the PO what they learned from the collages and what they'd like to know more about. Sense readiness and energy.

Next step. Recommended: reverge by having everyone present their collage in one minute (see Elevator Pitch). Or converge on new insights (e.g. Restating the Problem), diverge from the collages (e.g. Brainwriting with Post-its), take a break, or set actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• It's about playing and letting ideas come, not jumping to conclusions.
• A title helps people reflect on and sum up their work.
• Bring roughly twice as many magazines as participants.
• Pick magazines unrelated to the topic to force metaphorical thinking.
• People can go back to the magazines while composing.
• Some feel "not artsy" or find it childish. Show confidence in the technique, explain the purpose carefully, and consider an artefact-making icebreaker first.
• Have people note ideas, insights and questions during the presentations; you can flow straight into Brainwriting.
variants:
• Introduction through collages: people make a collage to introduce themselves, optionally on a theme. Useful when they'll work closely together afterwards.
• Guided Fantasy with collages (Segal, 2001): after a Guided Fantasy, pull images or ads that connect to what people visualised; after 5 to 10 minutes, build a collage.
background: From the French coller, to stick. Japanese artists have used collage alongside calligraphy for over 1,000 years. It was a Victorian folk art and was later taken up by avant-garde artists like Picasso and Braque (Butler-Kisber, 2008). Brockelman (2001) studies collage in postmodern art. It moved into qualitative research as a way to surface unconscious thoughts and to reflect and conceptualise. Tassoul (2009) suggests ways to use it in creative sessions.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.20, pp. 116-119

name: MATEC
diamondNote: Idea Finding
typeOfProblem: Single (problems that need really novel solutions)
materials: Flip-over sheets, masking tape, Post-its, markers
purpose:
Combines chain association (fluency) with Creative Confrontation (flexibility). It's eclectic like Synectics but simpler and more systematic. First, lots of word associations from the PaP's key terms gradually lead thinking away from the obvious, which works as a warm-up. Then two random words from those associations are combined and pushed into forced fitting.

Use it to:
• Give the RG a strong, easy example of Creative Confrontation.
• Raise the group's energy.
• Generate options beyond the obvious.
inShort: Choose three key terms from the PaP. For each, build a 5×5 grid of word associations through several chain associations. Pick two words at random from two different grids and force-fit them to find what they share or how they connect. Then relate those connections back to the PaP and force-fit again to generate options. The energizers (chain association, forced fitting) are built in.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaP. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Position the RG. Stand around the flip chart; markers for everyone.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge (if not done yet). One option per Post-it.
Explain the technique. Purpose and outcome.
Top row. With the RG, choose three key terms from the PaP. Write the first in the top-left corner and build a horizontal chain association until there are five column headings.
Fill the columns. From each heading, chain-associate downwards to complete the 5×5 grid. Repeat steps 6 and 7 for the other two key terms.
Excursion. Circle two words at random and write them at the top of a blank sheet. Ask what they share or how they connect; aim for at least five links.
Explain forced fitting. Purpose and outcome.

Force-fit. Take one link and ask what ideas it suggests for the PaP, or what it makes people think of in relation to the PaP. Capture options. Repeat with other links, then pick two new words and repeat steps 8 to 10.
Check on progress. Guard the mindset; check with the PO every 15 to 25 options.
Reflect. Target reached? Does the PO need more, and is the field covered?
Next step. Reverge, take a break, or set actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Associations should be drawable words; alternating words and pictures deepens thinking.
• Forced fitting asks a lot of the RG, so allow enough time.
• Pick the two words from different grids and far apart, with no obvious link.
• Run the whole procedure yourself beforehand to practise.
• Grid building (book Figure 3.1): a horizontal chain from keyword 1 gives the five headings, then vertical chains from each heading fill the columns. Repeat for keywords 2 and 3.
variants:
• Chain association: the basic version. Build one chain from a key word in or near the problem, pick a word from it, and force-fit it straight to the problem.
• Creative Confrontation: MATEC is a case of it. The grids and forced links are the excursion; the forced-fitting procedure is the same.
background: Developed in the 1970s by J.P. Sol at the French consultancy Créargie (Sol, 1974). The name stands for MATrice d'Eloignement Creatif, "Creative Distancing Matrix". COCD promoted it in Dutch-speaking regions (Vanosmael & De Bruyn, 1989), where it was popular in the 1990s, but it's missing from the newer book by de Bruyn's successors (Byttebier & Vullings, 2007). Tassoul (2009) describes it well.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.21, pp. 120-123

name: Mind Mapping in a Group Session
diamondNote: Mainly Problem Finding, sometimes Idea Finding
typeOfProblem: Complex (problems with abstract concepts or terminology)
materials: A3 and flip chart paper, markers, tape
website: Mind Mapping as a method; Tony Buzan video
purpose:
Maps an individual's or group's thinking around a topic. It was designed for organising and memorising thoughts individually, but it works in groups too. This version is especially good for building a broader, shared understanding of an abstract term in the PaG.

Use it to:
• Explore the context around a topic or problem.
• Build a shared memory, e.g. of every aspect of an abstract term in the PaG.
• Capture many-sided information in a structured way.
inShort: Write the PaG term the RG needs to understand better in the middle of a large sheet. Everyone gets a marker and branches out related words from the centre in a tree.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaG. The PO explains it, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Set the group and hand out supplies. Around a large table with an A2 or flip-over sheet. Post-its and black plus coloured markers for everyone.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge on the PaG (if not done yet). One option per Post-it; when it slows (5 to 10 minutes), ask for one more.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.

Start the map. Pick a word or topic from the PaG that needs clarifying and write it in the centre. Everyone adds associations, linking each to the word that triggered it. Continue until there's a broad picture of the topic and its relationships.
Check on progress. Guard the divergent mindset.
Reflect. Ask the PO whether more is needed, whether the field is covered, and what to explore further. Sense readiness and energy.

Next step. Reverge (e.g. the PO presents the map and sums up insights), converge on key aspects (e.g. Hits or Dots, then Restating the Problem), explore a direction further, take a break, or set actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Use it when a term in the PaG needs clarifying. In "Design packaging formats for e-commerce", people will read "e-commerce" differently; a map builds shared understanding and yields useful material for later.
• One word per branch keeps it divergent; sentences pull people into logical, convergent thinking.
• Encourage colours, symbols and specific words over generic ones.
• Avoid boxes around words: boxing words in tends to box in fluency too.
• With a large RG, split into groups of 3 to 5 and add debrief time.
• It was designed as an individual tool, so people can also make personal maps as quiet reflection before H2's or Restating the Problem.
• Combines well with 5W1H.
• Hang the finished map where everyone can see it.
variants:
• Flower Association is the most basic form. More uses on the website.
• Concept mapping (Novak, early 1970s): uses several key terms in a network to show complex connections and interdependencies. Put key terms on Post-its, arrange them on a flip chart, draw linking arrows, and label each link.
• Mind Mapping as excursion: start from a PaP keyword (or any random word) and map purely by association, at least five per branch, to get distance. Pick a word from the outer branches and force-fit it to the PaP (see Creative Confrontation).
background: Mind-map-like diagrams go back thousands of years; Porphyry of Tyre organised Aristotle's works as a "tree of knowledge" in the third century (Guerrero & Ramos, 2015). Novak developed what became concept mapping in 1972. Tony Buzan coined and trademarked "mind map", formalised the rules, and commercialised it with great success (Buzan, 1984; Buzan & Buzan, 1993). In iCPS it's most useful for structuring data in Information Finding, analysing the problem in Problem Finding, and generating ideas in Idea Finding.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.22, pp. 124-127

name: Morphological Synthesis
diamondNote: Mainly Idea Finding, sometimes Solution Finding
typeOfProblem: Complex (design of a product or process, especially in engineering)
materials: Morphological matrix on worksheet or flip chart, Post-its, markers, tape
purpose:
A systematic way to spark new thinking by combining existing elements from several parameters in new ways, using a matrix.

Use it to:
• Drive incremental change or improvement.
• Explore new combinations within a given structure.
• Produce many possible solutions from only a few parameters.
inShort: List 3 to 5 relevant attributes, functions or characteristics of the PaP (the parameters) down the left side of a large sheet. Next to each, write about five forms or variants (the elements), giving a matrix. Combining one element from each parameter, often at random, generates options. Five parameters with five elements each already give over three thousand combinations.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaP. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Position the RG and hand out supplies. Stand around a large sheet on the wall; Post-its and a marker each; ask for legible writing.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge (if not done yet). One option per Post-it; when it slows (5 to 10 minutes), ask for one more.
Explain the technique. Purpose and outcome.
Identify parameters. The RG names all attributes or variables of the product or process, one per Post-it. The PO picks 3 to 5 key, independent ones for the left column and clarifies what each means.
Generate elements. For each parameter, the RG names about five real alternatives, listed beside it to form the matrix.

Combine. Randomly circle one element per row. Ask what you get when you cross them, or what the combination suggests. The RG captures options in words or sketches on Post-its, which go on a blank flip chart. Repeat until there are enough options.
Check on progress. Guard the mindset; ask the PO whether options are the kind wanted.
Reflect. Target reached? Any combination the PO wants to explore further? Sense readiness.
Next step. More options, reverge, a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Use several flip charts so the matrix is large enough to read.
• Parameters should be at the same level of abstraction and independent of each other, to avoid conflicting combinations.
• More elements means more complexity; aim for 4 to 6 per parameter and focus on the most interesting if there are many.
• Use feasible, existing elements. The novelty is in the unexpected combination, not in any single element.
• Number rows and columns so you can pick at random, e.g. with dice.
• You can start from an option (idea, solution or concept) from an earlier diamond and elaborate on it.
• Works best for products, services and processes.
variants:
• Other names: morphological creativity, morphological matrix, morphological chart, morphological grid.
• Attribute listing (Crawford, 1954): just the first step, as its own technique. Break an existing product or process into attributes and ask how to change, modify or improve each (e.g. with SCAMPER questions).
• Function analysis (L.D. Miles, 1961, from Value Engineering): the parameters are functions, each written as an active verb plus a measurable noun (a light bulb "illuminates area"). Elements answer "What else would do the job?" Good for uncovering hidden presumptions.
• The Allen morphologizer (Allen, 1962): a thorough way to find parameters using cards or Post-its, reverged step by step into at most seven clusters (the elements).
background: In biology, morphology is the study of the structure and form of organisms; you can identify a plant from its characteristics. Listing every parameter also lets you explore all their combinations. Fritz Zwicky introduced this "general morphology" in the late 1940s (Zwicky, 1969). Allen (1961) brought it into creative problem solving, and others (e.g. Parnes, 1976) turned it into a session technique. The entertainment industry uses similar approaches to map out plots for games, films and TV (Grasbon & Braun, 2001).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.23, pp. 128-131

name: Picture the Problem
diamondNote: Problem Finding
materials: Large flip-over sheets, coloured markers, masking tape
purpose:
Makes participants use their imagination to picture the problem and its context. It's especially good at surfacing aspects that would feel too confronting or threatening to say out loud.

Use it to:
• Describe the problem in pictures instead of words.
• Open up a problem the RG feels is stuck.
• Surface hidden or threatening aspects of the problem or situation.
• Build a shared understanding of the problem and its context.
inShort: In subgroups of about three, participants make quick A4 sketches and doodles of the PaG and its context from different angles. Once each subgroup has about ten, they combine the main insights into one big drawing. Presenting and discussing these posters in plenary (reverging) leads to reformulating the PaG as the PaP.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaG. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Form subgroups and hand out supplies. Groups of about three, each with a large sheet (A2 or flip-over), a pile of A4 and coloured markers.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge on the PaG (if not done yet). One option per Post-it; when it slows (5 to 10 minutes), ask for one more.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.

Draw. Explain that they'll make a poster, but first everyone does quick individual A4 sketches of the problem. If groups start discussing, tell them to just start drawing different aspects, and that what they draw matters, not how. Push for new drawings rather than perfecting one, and remind them hitchhiking is welcome.
Merge into a poster. After ten or more sketches, each subgroup groups them by theme and makes one big drawing of its key insights.
Reflect. Ask the PO what they learned.
Next step. Recommended: reverge by having each subgroup present (see Elevator Pitch), then converge with Restating the Problem. Or allow reflection time, a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Encourage metaphors; they raise issues without confrontation.
• Keep words in the drawings to a minimum.
• Skip perspective and shading if they slow things down.
• Warm up with a sketching exercise or energizer.
• Prompts for varied sketches: a bird's-eye view, a caricature, a metaphor, a diagram, the problem ten years from now, someone else's view (end user, outsider, expert, child, alien), or the variables with lines showing how they interact.
variants:
• Other names: rich picture, draw your problem, sketch the problem.
• Ask for a storyboard or infographic instead of a drawing.
• Lego Serious Play (Kristiansen & Rasmussen, 2014): build the problem with Lego or other bricks. Like sketching, making small artefacts makes ideas tangible and grounds focused reflection and discussion.
background: A variant of Brainsketching (Pickens, 1980; van der Lugt, 2001), developed for analysing complex problems because it guides non-verbal thinking and supports discussion (Ferguson, 1992). Sketching puts every facet on paper, which acts as an extension of the brain and frees working memory to find the essence (Bilda & Gero, 2007). It also builds mutual understanding, shown neatly by Tom Wujec's DrawToast exercise (2018), which also works as an energizer to start the technique.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.24, pp. 132-135

name: SCAMPER
diamondNote: Any
typeOfProblem: Single (clearly defined problem statement; incremental change)
materials: Markers, Post-its, flip chart
purpose:
A set of questions that boosts the flexibility and/or fluency of options, getting the RG to think about the PaP in new ways.

Use it to:
• Steer the flow of options in new directions (flexibility).
• Generate options beyond the obvious.
• Keep options coming when fluency drops (as a fluency enhancer).
inShort: The facilitator asks a series of "What if we X?" questions, filling X from the SCAMPER checklist: Substitute; Combine; Adapt; Modify (maximise or minimise); Put to other uses or change perspective; Eliminate; Reverse.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaP. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Position the RG and hand out supplies. Stand around a large sheet on the wall; Post-its and a marker each; ask for clear, short writing.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge and generate. Everyone writes whatever comes to mind, as in Brainwriting with Post-its. When fluency drops, switch to the provocations.
Introduce SCAMPER. Purpose and outcome, a few example questions, then answer questions.
Provoke. Ask questions like "What if we substitute…?" or "What if we combine… and…?" while the RG writes down whatever comes up. Give each question enough time; move on when it's saturated.
Check on progress. Guard the mindset; ask the PO whether options are heading the right way.
Reflect. Target reached? Does the PO need more, is the field covered, what to explore further? Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. More options, reverge, a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• This version is structured because the focus is flexibility; introduce each step properly and give the RG enough time.
• It can be even more structured as an excursion (see Creative Confrontation).
• As a pure fluency enhancer, skip step 5 to keep things fast and spontaneous. Don't take the questions too literally; drop them in lightly and seemingly at random.
• Use the questions in any order or combination; you don't need them all, and you can add your own.
• One flip chart per question, with the group posting its options there.
• In Idea Finding it's great for redesigning existing products, services or systems; in Solution Finding for elaborating concepts. Start from the product or option instead of the PaP.
• In Problem Finding, use it to probe the edges of the problem space and challenge the PaG.
variants:
Many provocation lists exist; the long ones resemble Osborn's original and the clustered ones resemble SCAMPER. For example:
• 5 Templates by SIT (Goldenberg et al., 1999): Systematic Inventive Thinking, which builds on TRIZ. Subtract, multiply, divide, unify, make or dissolve dependencies.
• Action verbs (Lupton, 2011): magnify, minify, multiply, flatten, stretch, invert, scale up or down, fatten, change materialisation, combine, explode, squeeze, melt.
• Manipulative verbs (Koberg & Bagnall, 1974): a long list, including divide, eliminate, invert, separate, transpose, unify, distort, rotate, freeze, soften, by-pass, repeat, extrude, protect, integrate, symbolise, abstract.

Many stand-alone techniques are really SCAMPER with one question:
• Reverse brainstorming (de Bono, 1992): take the usual way of doing something and suggest the exact opposite.
• Absurd exaggeration (Olson, 1980): push any normal measure (number, frequency, weight, volume, temperature, duration) far outside its usual range.
background: Osborn (1953) already used provocative questions to keep option generation going in brainstorming; he wrote over eighty idea-spurring questions. Eberle (1971) grouped them into seven clusters under the SCAMPER mnemonic. Later Buffalo scholars kept only the strongest: magnify, minimise, rearrange (Parnes, 1997). Later lists like SIT's 5 Templates (Goldenberg et al., 1999) and Lupton's Action Verbs (2011) closely resemble it.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.25, pp. 136-139

name: 40 Inventive Principles of TRIZ
diamondNote: Idea Finding
materials: Flip chart, markers, Post-its, preselected inventive TRIZ principles including examples
website: TRIZ the method, examples, selection tool
purpose:
The same problems and solutions turn up across industries and sciences, so TRIZ offers a systematic way to solve (mainly technical) problems. Technical challenges are often contradictions, like making a car accelerate faster without a bigger engine. Applying one or more of the 40 principles gives a new way to look at the PaP. TRIZ as a whole is complex; this is a simplified slice of it.

Use it to:
• Tackle PaPs that contain a striking paradox.
• Modify or improve existing products, services and systems in the second diamond.
• Strengthen promising ideas or concepts in the third diamond.
• Find solutions from outside the field they were developed in.
inShort: The principles are used as stimuli for more ideas. Before the session, the facilitator picks 3 to 8 of the 40 based on contradictions in the PaG. In the session, each principle is introduced in turn and the RG uses it to generate ideas for the PaP.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaP. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
