Hand out supplies. Post-its and markers each; ask for clear, short writing.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge (if not done yet). One option per Post-it; when it slows (5 to 10 minutes), ask for one more.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.

Apply a principle. Explain one preselected principle briefly with an example. Ask how the problem could be solved by applying it, or what would happen if we did. The RG notes options on Post-its. If fluency drops or the principle feels too hard, switch to another. Repeat until the principles are used up or there are enough options.
Check on progress. Guard the mindset; ask the PO whether options are heading the right way.
Reflect. Target reached? Does the PO need more, is the field covered, what to explore further? Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. More options, reverge, a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Preselect the best-fitting principles beforehand by reading all 40 or using the contradiction matrix (www.triz40.com has a selection tool).
• Plan how to present each principle, e.g. with examples and pictures. Play with them yourself first.
• Don't overload the RG with information on any single principle.
• TRIZ stresses analysing the problem space, so start with a Problem Finding technique to get to the root.
variants:
• TIPS (Theory of Inventive Problem Solving): TRIZ under another name.
• SIT or ASIT ((Advanced) Systematic Inventive Thinking), by Dr. Roni Horowitz to address some TRIZ drawbacks. Reduces the 40 principles to five mechanisms: unification, multiplication, division, breaking symmetry, object removal. Very close to SCAMPER.
• ARIZ (Algorithm to Solve an Inventive Problem): TRIZ's main analytical tool, a step-by-step route to solutions for complex problems (Altshuller, 2005).
• TRIZ Lines of Evolution (Altshuller): generate ideas by imagining a product's next evolutionary form. Eight lines: life cycle, dynamisation, multiplication cycle (to bi- or poly-system), macro to micro, synchronisation, scaling up or down, uneven development of parts, replacing the human (automation). See Langevin (2013); apply it like SCAMPER.
• TRIZ beyond technical systems: now applied to business cases, service systems, even food (e.g. triz-journal.com).
background: Genrich Altshuller started TRIZ in the USSR in 1946; the Russian acronym means "theory of inventive problem solving" (Altshuller & Shapiro, 1956). He studied thousands of patents, found recurring patterns, and distilled 40 inventive principles. Most patents resolve a technical contradiction (improving one parameter without worsening another), so he built a contradiction matrix pointing to the most relevant principles (Altshuller, 2005). Modern TRIZ covers the whole creative problem-solving process, which it calls the "Systematic Innovation Process".
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.26, pp. 140-143

name: 5W1H
diamondNote: Mainly Problem Finding, sometimes Idea and Solution Finding
typeOfProblem: Complex (especially social and societal rather than technical)
materials: Flip-over sheets, tape, black markers, Post-its
purpose:
A checklist for analysing the PaG: Who, What, Where, When, Why and How. It gathers facts and data for a rich description of the problem. It's really an Information Finding activity that fits inside Problem Finding, and it's also very useful in the intake with the PO before the session.

Use it to:
• Gather information on the problem and solution space.
• Get a thorough understanding of the problem.
• Spot underlying problems or patterns.
inShort: Use question words to ask things like: why is there a problem, who owns it, who has an interest in solving it, what is the actual problem, what causes it, why is there no solution yet, when did it start, where is it? Answer them together with the PO and anyone closely involved. The answers are usually facts, not ideas or problems; rearranging them can reveal new insights or patterns. Finish with "How?", e.g. how was it handled before, or how should a new solution be implemented?

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write up the PaG. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a desired solution, and answers questions.
Hand out supplies. A black marker and Post-its each; ask for clear, short writing.
Set the divergent mindset. Postpone judgment; recap quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel.
Purge (if not done yet). One option per Post-it; when it slows (5 to 10 minutes), ask for one more.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.
List the questions. With the PO (and possibly the RG), write W-questions about the problem on a flip chart, starting with Who, What, Where, When and Why.
Answer the W-questions. The PO answers one by one in front of the RG, bringing in the RG or experts if needed. Each answer goes on its own Post-it next to its question.
Answer the H-question. The whole RG, PO included, answers How questions to trigger first options (e.g. how it was handled before, how a new solution should be implemented).
Check on progress. Guard the mindset; ask the PO whether options are heading the right way.
Reflect. Is the field covered? Anything to explore further? Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. Reverge the information (e.g. Spontaneous Clustering), reformulate the problem with H2's and Restating the Problem, take a break, or set actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Use it very early in Problem Finding.
• Also useful when building an action plan or implementation strategy.
• Add provocations like "What if…?" and "How else…?"
• A mind map works well as the format for the 5 W's and H.
• Also works as a fluency enhancer in any diverging technique (e.g. Brainwriting with Post-its), as a checklist for criteria in converging techniques, and in the PO intake.
variants:
• Other names: WWWWWH, the W-train (Booreiland, 2013).
• Interviewing: write your own question list and use it as a checklist in the session or the PO intake.
• Ladder of Abstraction: "Why?" makes the problem statement broader and more abstract; "How?" makes it narrower and more concrete.
background: Hermagoras of Temnos, a Greek rhetorician of the second century BC, defined seven "circumstances" as sources of information on an issue: who, what, when, where, why, in what way, and by what means (Dieter & Kurth, 1968). The approach shaped many Greek and Latin authors and later became standard for orators, confessors and journalists. It's often linked to Kipling's poem (1902) about six honest serving men named What, Why, When, How, Where and Who.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.1.27, pp. 144-147

name: Idea Gallery
diamondNote: Any
materials: Masking tape, generated options on Post-its, large wall, flip chart
purpose:
Options that someone doesn't understand tend to get cut when the group converges. That can be down to messy handwriting, a half-written spark from a fast diverging round, or an idea that's simply too new to grasp at first glance. Diverging is not the moment to explain, so Idea Gallery gives every option a second look. Talking each one through also makes it grow on the group, which raises its chance of surviving selection.

Use it to:
• Give every option attention.
• Clear up what each option means.
inShort: All options go up on a big wall in random order, each with a number. The facilitator reads them out one at a time and checks whether the RG needs clarification, writing any notes beside the option. By the end the group shares an understanding of the full set and is ready to converge.

stepByStep.text: Set up the room. Move the options into one or more numbered columns on a large wall everyone can see. Leave space beside each for notes.
Explain the process. Purpose, outcome, the steps in brief; answer questions.
Prepare the RG. Read the PaP aloud, bring the group to the wall, and remind them of the reverging mindset: inquire, don't judge.
Revisit each option. Read it aloud and invite questions about what it means and the thinking behind it. If it still seems unclear, ask someone to expand on it until it is.
Check on progress. Watch that people stay curious rather than critical.
Reflect. Confirm every option was covered. Ask the PO whether they're happy with the set, want to add anything, or see gaps. Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. More diverging, move on to converging, a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Works with 1 to 50 options.
• Photograph the raw options before moving them into columns; include it in the session report.
• Keep spare flip-over sheets on the wall.
• Encourage clarification, not debate.
• New ideas that pop up go on fresh Post-its too.
• Rewrite illegible options on a new Post-it stuck over the original.
variants: • Presenting options: with roughly 10 to 20 options, have the author pitch each in a single sentence. Keeps pace and energy up and forces focus on what's unique. Suits Solution Finding, where options are developed concepts.
background: Reading every option aloud is the most basic form of reverging and long-standing facilitator practice, but the authors say this is its first written description. The Nominal Group Technique (Delbecq & Van de Ven, 1971) has a similar step.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.2.1, pp. 150-153

name: Elevator Pitch
diamondNote: Solution Finding
materials: Masking tape, A3 sheets, markers
purpose:
When pairs or subgroups have worked out concepts separately (for example with Making a Poster), the whole RG needs to see them all. A strict time limit makes presenters cut to the core and name what makes their option special, and the quick rhythm keeps energy up.

Use it to:
• Share several developed options across the RG.
• Make the case for a particular option.
• Get ready for converging.
• Keep momentum and energy.
inShort: Bring everyone back together and give each pair or subgroup one minute to pitch. A pitch covers three things: the problem, the solution, and what makes it unique. The RG then asks clarifying questions before the next pitch.

stepByStep.text: Set up the room. Mark out one or more "stages". Write the pitch recipe on a flip chart: about one minute (roughly 150 words) covering problem, solution, and what's unique.
Explain the process. Purpose, outcome, steps; answer questions.
Prepare the RG. Read the PaP aloud. Each pair or subgroup gets about ten minutes to prepare. Coach them to open strongly, cover the three parts, and close with a memorable one-liner.
Pitch. The audience sits in a half circle around the stage; the first presenters get their minute.
Questions, one minute max. Remind everyone to inquire rather than judge, then move to the next pitch.
Reflect. Were all options covered? Check with the PO for satisfaction, additions and gaps. Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. Rework pitches based on feedback, diverge further, converge, take a break, or set actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Keep it brisk; go straight to the next pitch.
• Instead of one stage, move the RG to different rooms or corners per pitch. The movement and change of scene keep people alert.
• The opening line matters most: hook the audience with a provocation, question, challenge or surprising fact.
• Describe the problem before the solution.
• O'Leary's 9 C's (book Figure 3.4) work as a checklist: concise, clear, compelling, credible, conceptual, concrete, consistent, customized, conversational.
variants:
• Other names: elevator speech, elevator statement.
• Pitch practice: use it to rehearse for Acceptance Finding, preparing the RG to win over outsiders later.
background: Born as an entrepreneur's tool: be ready to pitch an idea to an executive or investor in the length of a lift ride. First in print with Philip Crosby (1981) as an "elevator speech". Milo Frank (1986) wrote about getting a point across in 30 seconds. O'Leary (2008) stresses that the aim is to open a conversation, not close a sale.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.2.2, pp. 154-157. Starting point: the RG has developed one or more options in pairs or subgroups.

name: Spontaneous Clustering
diamondNote: Mainly Problem and Idea Finding, sometimes Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, tape, options on Post-its, markers
purpose:
Help the RG move from the energetic diverging stage to the calm, focused converging stage. With 50+ options, clustering builds shared understanding and an overview.

Use it to:
• Get an overview of all options.
• Shift the group into a calmer, considering mood.
• Bring order to a large set of options.
• Judge whether to converge now or diverge a bit longer.
inShort: The RG links options and groups similar ones. Categories emerge on the spot, based on any similarity: form, function, working principle, target group. Each cluster gets a catchy, metaphorical name.

stepByStep.text: Prepare the room. All options on Post-its, all on the wall, visible to everyone.
Explain the technique. Purpose, spontaneity, steps, questions.
Prepare the RG. Read the PaG or PaP aloud. Everyone stands at the wall. Repeat the reverging mindset and rules: use the inquiring mind, be jointly active, listen responsively, move circularly.

Get going. Involve everyone: grab a Post-it, find a similar one, place them close together, move things freely. Group by feeling and intuition, not by preset lists. Add an "other" cluster for leftovers.
Name each cluster with a catchy name on a Post-it in a different colour.
Check progress. Watch the mindset. Near the end ask the PO: do the clusters cover the field? Want more options in a cluster? An area to explore further?
Present. A volunteer walks through the clusters. PO and RG add remarks.
Reflect. All options revisited? PO happy with the overview? Gaps? Ready for the next step? Energy?
Decide the next step. Extra diverging in a cluster or gap, converging, a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Works best when diverging used Post-its.
• Usually five to seven clusters emerge, plus "other".
• Put plenty of empty sheets on the wall. 100 to 200 ideas need at least seven sheets.
• No interruptions or breaks during clustering.
• Stay out of the content completely.
• Capture new ideas that pop up on new Post-its.
• Use catchy, metaphorical names. Avoid generic terms.
• Before converging, take a short break and an energizer if needed.
• An option fits two clusters? Duplicate it.
variants:
• Predefined categories: the facilitator or, better, the RG sets overarching themes first.
• Verb-phrase names (Firestien, 2018): "emphasize local quality" instead of "local quality". More actionable.
• KJ / TKJ / affinity diagramming: everyone writes facts and ideas on cards. Cards get shuffled and redistributed. The facilitator reads one card, others add similar ones from their pile. Each set gets a name capturing its essence. Set names are used to restate the problem. Anonymous by design (Kawakita, 1977; Higgins, 1994).
background: Classic CPS went straight from diverging to converging. At Delft, large option sets (50+) made groups lose overview, so clustering was added as a mental pause (Tassoul & Buijs, 2007). Heijne and Smit (2018) later named the whole in-between stage "reverging".
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.2.3, pp. 158-161

name: Sequencing
diamondNote: Any
materials: Masking tape, generated options on Post-its, large wall, flip-over sheets
website: The book's website lists more techniques with sequencing built in
purpose:
The RG revisits every option and places it along one or two axes (rarely a third). Each axis stands for a parameter chosen to suit the goal. The result is an overview of the full set in relation to those parameters, plus a shared understanding of it.

Use it to:
• Draw attention to a particular kind of option.
• Find blind spots in the set.
• Look at all options as a whole.
inShort: Draw a scale (one axis) or a matrix (two axes) on the wall and label it. Agree with the RG what each axis really means. The RG then places every option, looking for agreement on where each belongs. Once everything is placed, analyse and discuss the picture.

stepByStep.text: Set up the room. Check all options are on Post-its and visible on the wall. Draw a large scale or matrix; label the axes and their two extremes.
Explain the process. Purpose, outcome, steps; answer questions.
Prepare the RG. Read the PaG or PaP aloud, bring everyone to the wall, and recap the reverging rules: inquire, stay jointly active, listen, move around.
Get going. Everyone takes Post-its, reads them, and places them on the axes. Moving someone else's option is fine.
Check on progress. Guard the reverging mindset; ask the PO whether there are blind spots on the scale or matrix.
Reflect. Were all options placed? Ask the PO whether the overview works, what they'd add, and which area needs more options or exploration. Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. Follow the C-Box or SML routes below, diverge to fill gaps, converge, take a break, or set actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Works best when the diverging stage used Post-its.
• Keep spare flip-over sheets on the wall.
• No interruptions or breaks mid-activity.
• Stay out of the content entirely.
• New ideas that come up go on Post-its too.
• Sequencing often sits inside hybrid techniques (C-Box, SML); keep the reverging part clearly separate from the diverging or converging part around it.
• Before converging afterwards, take a short break, plus an energizer if needed.
• A pyramid or target can replace straight axes to show hierarchy more clearly.
• Options placed close together on an axis aren't necessarily related.
• Agree on axis labels in plenary, since most can be read in several ways. Majaro (1988) gives examples: attractiveness (originality, simplicity, ease of implementation…) and compatibility (with budget, people, corporate image, protectability…).
variants:
Many techniques have sequencing built in: roadmapping, FCB grid, screening matrix for ideas, WOW-matrix, brand/innovation matrix, innovation matrix, MoSCoW and more (see the book's website). Their labels can inspire your axes. The book singles out two:

C-Box (3.2.4.a)

Answers the "creadox", the paradox of creativity (Byttebier et al., 2007): the RG aims for originality while diverging, then drops the novel ideas while converging because they look too hard. Place options on originality (common to original) against feasibility (easy to difficult to implement; think cost, legality, technology, strategy). The three quadrants of interest are NOW (easy, common), WOW! (easy, original) and HOW? (difficult, original). Follow-up routes:

1. Diverge: take an original but hard option and ask the RG what would move it towards easy to implement, or which related ideas would be easier (e.g. with Interactive Brainsketching). Rewrite changed options on new Post-its.
2. Converge: protect novelty, e.g. with Hits or Dots. The sweet spot is often where NOW, WOW! and HOW? meet: original enough to matter, close enough to build.

SML (3.2.4.b)

Short, Medium, Long (Isaksen, Dorval & Treffinger, 2000). A timeline for ending a session and preparing for action: place an already converged set of options along a time axis. Follow-up routes:

1. Wrap up: turn it into an action plan with names, resources and deadlines (who takes which option forward?).
2. Diverge: for long-term options, ask what the group should start now to prepare.
background: The authors coined "Sequencing" for every reverging technique that rearranges options along one axis (scale), two (matrix) or three (cube). Heijne and Smit (2018) studied existing examples and found most embedded in hybrids that pair sequencing with a diverging or converging step. Scale example: SML. Matrix example: the screening matrix for ideas (Majaro, 1988; Higgins, 1994), which became the C-Box. Cubes are rarely used because they're complex.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.2.4, pp. 162-167

name: Restating the Problem
diamondNote: Problem Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, tape, black marker, large Post-its and a marker per person
purpose:
Reach a good PaP after exploring the PaG, for example with 5W1H, Picture the Problem or H2's. A weak PaP means weak options later, however good the session.

Use it to:
• Find a strong starting point for the second diamond.
• Look at the PaG from different viewpoints.
• Define a PaP the whole RG understands and supports.
inShort: After analysing the PaG, the RG writes 15 to 20 reformulations. The PO picks 1 to 3 to work on. Shape the result with SPARK.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write the PaG visibly. Explore it by questioning the PO. PO answers RG questions.
Hand out supplies. Post-its and markers.
Purge if not done. One option per Post-it, one more after the flow drops (5 to 10 min).
Explain the technique. Purpose, steps, questions.
Write restatements. Each person writes their understanding of the PaG as "How to..." statements, one per Post-it. Target about 15 to 20.
Check progress with the PO: right direction, enough options, field covered?

PO selects 1 to 3 statements that capture the essence or deserve rework. Remind the PO of the converging mindset: affirmative judgment, protect originality, trust the hedonic response, have action in mind.
Rework with the whole RG. Decide if one statement suffices. Check against SPARK.
Check again. Does this PaP capture the essence? Would the PO be satisfied if we answered it? Is it a good entry for the second diamond?
Write the final PaP on the wall.
Reflect. Ready for the next step? Energy?
Next step. Second diamond, a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Step 5 is a diverging step. Extend it with H2's.
• Against Creadox when the PO picks, ask: "If we manage this, will it make you happy?" This pushes bolder statements.
• Complex problems may need more than one PaP. Split the RG or extend the session.
• Repeat the technique later if second-diamond options miss what the PO wants.
• A well-defined PaG makes this quicker, but still rework with the whole RG.
variants: Also known as redefining, reformulating, reframing, re-boxing, goal orientation.
background: A strong starting point is vital for complex open problems (Ma, 2009). All later work solves the problem "as named" (Kepner & Tregoe). Engaging the RG in reformulating raises quality and originality (Mumford et al., 1994). Wording shapes the approach people take (Ward, 2004). SPARK builds on Osborn's "one single concrete target".
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.3.1, pp. 170-173

name: Hits or Dots
diamondNote: Mainly Problem and Idea Finding, sometimes Solution Finding
materials: Small bright stickers (dots) or markers
purpose:
A focusing technique built on experience, personal judgment and intuition. One of the most used tools to screen hundreds of options.

Use it to:
• Screen promising options from a long list.
• Select options for further work.
inShort: Each person uses inner criteria to mark promising options. The guiding question: which ones are on target, intriguing, or feel like the best bets? Often the first focusing step on large sets.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Read the PaP on the wall aloud. PO answers questions if needed.
Set up. RG stands around the options. Each person gets dots (see tips for how many).
Set the convergent mindset. Affirmative judgment. Rules: protect novelty, trust the hedonic response, have action in mind.
Explain the technique. Purpose, steps, questions.
Define a hit. Ask the PO for criteria. Without criteria, use the general traits of a hit (book Figure 3.8).
Dot the hits. In silence, green dots on options that feel right or intriguing. Give one or two red dots for novel hits only, to protect novelty.
Interpret. Ask the PO what the dots say and which options need more thought.
Reflect. Ready? Energy?
Next step. Another converging tool such as UALo or a ranking, maybe another dot round. Or a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Number of dots: bigger RG, fewer dots each. More options, more dots. Rule of thumb for 6 to 9 people: the square root of the number of options. 100 options gives 10 dots each.
• Stress it is not voting. It informs the PO about promising directions.
• People may skip near-duplicates of already dotted options.
• Allow stacking dots on one option to show priority.
• Optionally rank hits by dot count for an overview.
variants:
• Other names: selecting hits, multi-voting, dot-voting.
• Highlighting or Hot Spots: select hits, cluster them, then write a statement per cluster ("What we see ourselves doing is...") (Isaksen et al., 2000).
• COCD-box (Byttebier, 2007): blue, red, yellow dots for Now, Wow and How ideas, mapped on a feasibility vs novelty 2x2.
• Low hanging fruit: red, green, black dots for effort, revenue and own influence. Plot revenue vs effort. Low hanging fruit sits where revenue beats effort (Van Leeuwen & Terhürne, 2010).
background: Diverging techniques produced huge option sets, so converging had to scale. People always circled favourites, but the first formal write-up was "Highlighting" (Firestien & Treffinger, 1983). Also called "Head and shoulders". This version follows Buijs and van der Meer (2013).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.3.2, pp. 174-177. Starting point: 50+ reverged options.

name: Paired Comparison
diamondNote: Idea Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers, PC worksheet or prepared flip-over sheet
purpose:
Ranks options by weighing each against every other, one pair at a time.

Use it to:
• Compare and rank a moderate number of options.
• Help the RG agree on priorities.
inShort: Also called Paired Comparison Analysis (PCA). First make the options fair to compare and tag each with a keyword or two. Each RG member fills in a personal grid, choosing the more relevant option in every pair. The individual totals go onto a shared flip chart, which becomes the basis for a group discussion about priority.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Write the PaP up large. The PO explains the task, gives an example of a good outcome, and answers questions.
Hand out supplies. Markers and a worksheet each; ask for clear, short writing.
Set the convergent mindset. Affirmative judgment: protect novelty, trust the hedonic response, keep action in mind.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.
Prepare the options. Label them A, B, C… Reword where needed so they're parallel and distinct. Add one or two core keywords to each.
Compare individually. On the worksheet, each person works through every pair (A vs B, A vs C…) and writes down the letter they'd take forward. Then they count how often each letter was chosen.
Collect scores. On a flip-over sheet, list options down the side and RG members across the top. Everyone fills in their totals; add up each row.

Move to consensus. Circle the highest and lowest individual scores, then ask the RG to interpret the chart. Capture the discussion on a separate sheet and present scores and conclusions to the PO, who decides what goes forward.
Reflect. Does the PO want to dig into any scores? Are they comfortable proceeding? Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. Develop the chosen options (e.g. UALo or Interactive Brainsketching), move to Acceptance Finding, take a break, or set actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• Parallel means the same level of abstraction and the same framing (all positive or all negative). Distinct means little or no overlap.
• Open discussion needs trust. Keep the PO out of the scoring and present the result to them as advice; the PO makes the final call.
• To deepen the discussion, add strength of preference on a 1–3 scale (slightly, moderately, much more important), e.g. "A3". It adds complexity to manage.
• On paper it only works for a handful of options. Use Hits or Dots first to get from hundreds down to 5 to 10.
• In digital tools (e.g. Spilter, Stormz) it scales to hundreds of options. It then becomes far more intuitive than argumentative, and trusting the hedonic response matters even more.
• The book's Figure 3.9 shows the three sheets: option list, individual grid with totals, and group score table.
variants: • Elimination race (Van Leeuwen & Terhürne, 2010): compare two Post-its, keep the winner, and repeat until enough options remain. The downside is losing sight of the full set.
background: Thurstone (1927) proposed the law of comparative judgment for measuring psychological values. Bradley and Terry (1952) gave it the name Paired Comparison, now used for prioritising in many fields. Isaksen et al. (2000) report its use in creative facilitation from the 1970s and describe it for sessions.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.3.3, pp. 178-181

name: Criteria and Ranking
diamondNote: Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, black markers, C&R worksheet, prepared flip-over sheet
purpose:
C&R (Criteria & Ranking) helps a group agree on, and then apply, the standards it judges options by.

Use it to:
• Make evaluation standards explicit and easy to communicate.
• Understand what makes an option promising.
• Screen and prioritise promising options.
inShort: Two parts. First the group creates a set of criteria, going through diverging, reverging and converging in turn. Then those criteria become the yardstick for discussing and ranking the shortlisted options.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Read the PaP aloud; the PO answers questions.
Hand out supplies. Markers, Post-its and a worksheet each; ask for clear, short writing.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.

List criteria. Generate, reverge and select 5 to 10 criteria, using a suitable technique for each stage. Prompt with questions about what the options should be measured on and what qualities an ideal option has.
Score individually. Everyone except the PO writes the criteria and option keywords on their worksheet. They score each option per criterion from 5 (perfect) to 1 (poor) and total each option.
Collect scores. On a visible flip-over sheet, options go across the top and criteria down the side. Everyone copies in their scores; total each column.

Move to consensus. Circle the highest and lowest individual scores and ask the RG to interpret the chart. Note the discussion on a separate sheet, present scores and conclusions to the PO, and let the PO choose what goes forward.
Reflect. Does the PO want more detail on any scores? Comfortable proceeding? Sense the energy.
Next step. Develop the chosen options (e.g. UALo or Interactive Brainsketching), Acceptance Finding, a break, or actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• A common way to build criteria: Brainstorming, then Idea Gallery, then Hits or Dots.
• Start a draft criteria list with the PO during the intake.
• You can also make the list early in the session, before options exist. Recheck it before scoring, which often happens in Solution Finding.
• Discussion needs trust. Keep the PO out of the scoring and present the ranking as advice. Give each participant a different marker colour on the group sheet.
• Make criteria measurable by spelling out what each point on the scale means for this case (e.g. "perfect budget" = under €1000).
• On paper it only works for a few options. Narrow down first with Hits or Dots.
• Digital tools (e.g. Spilter, Stormz) make scoring 10+ options quick and convincing.
variants:
• Musts and Wants (Spitzer & Evans, 1997), common in companies: knock-out criteria every option must pass, then want criteria to score the survivors.
• Harris profile (Van Boeijen et al., 2014), common among designers: shows the scores graphically on a 4-point scale.
• MCA, multi-criteria analysis, common in technical fields: weight each criterion (often 1–5) and multiply. More refined, but weights can be tuned to produce any outcome you want.
• NAF (Nolan, 1989), from the Synectics community: three criteria (New, Attractive, Feasible) on a 10-point scale. Copied as NAA, IEF, NUF and others; the website has a digital NUF example.
background: Judging by criteria is ancient (de Boer, 1989). In CPS, Parnes (1967) discussed criteria and Isaksen et al. (2000) formalised C&R. Often used with a fixed set, e.g. NAF. Adding weights turns it into MCA; Cooper (1979) built NewProd on MCA with statistically derived criteria and weights. The authors prefer plain C&R because MCA is hard to run with groups and leans on subjective weights.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.3.4, pp. 182-185. Starting point: 5 to 10 preselected options.

name: UALo
diamondNote: Solution Finding
materials: UALo worksheet (book website), markers
purpose:
Investigate, polish and strengthen an option with affirmative judgment. People find negatives easily, especially in new ideas. Starting with the positives protects novelty in immature options.

Use it to:
• Evaluate and strengthen options.
• Stress the pros, then work on the cons.
• Protect novelty.
• Avoid Creadox, killing ideas too early.
inShort: The order is in the name. Unique qualities first, then advantages, then limitations. Limitations come as "How to...?" or "How might...?" questions to avoid a dump of negatives. Rank the limitations, then diverge on how to overcome them, or even turn them into advantages.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Read the PaP aloud. PO answers questions if needed.
Form subgroups of 2 or 3. One worksheet and markers each.
Set the convergent mindset. Protect novelty, trust the hedonic response, have action in mind.
Explain the technique. Purpose, steps, questions.
Demo with one option in plenary.
U, unique qualities. What makes this option unique? What does it have that others lack? Find the core to preserve.
A, advantages. At least three strengths. What do you like about it?
L, limitations. Only after the A list is done. Shortcomings, why it might fail. Phrase each as "How to...?"
o, overcome. Rank the limitation questions. Generate ideas for each, most important first. This part is diverging, so switch back to diverging rules.
Repeat in subgroups for the remaining options (steps 6 to 9).
Share outcomes in plenary.
Check progress with the PO: enough U's, A's, L's and o's? Need to know more about some options?
Reflect. More overcoming ideas needed? Ready? Energy?
Next step. Action plan, more diverging on limitations, or a break.

tipsAndTricks:
• Finish U and A before L.
• U is about the key unique element, not a long list.
• Watch for trivial pluses or strengths hiding weaknesses.
• Phrase limitations without negative words. "How to make it affordable?" beats "How to make it less expensive?"
• When overcoming limits, keep the unique elements intact.
• Common after Hits or Dots in Solution Finding.
• Headline each point in about 5 to 7 words.
• Optional: set criteria first to prompt U, A, L and o.
• If the PO joins throughout, skip subgroups.
• At session end, add an action plan: who, what, when, plus "the first next step".
variants:
• Itemized response / plus-minus (Synectics, Gordon 1961): three strengths, one concern as a question.
• PMI (De Bono, 1978): plusses, minuses, interesting.
• ALU (Isaksen & Treffinger, 1985): sandwich, negative between two positives. Good for structured feedback on anything.
• PPC / PPCo (Firestien et al., 1982, later with "o"): pluses, potentials, concerns, overcome.
• Others: Praise first, POINt, IPC, LCOb, PPH2.
background: Pros and cons with pros first. Builds on Synectics' itemized response and the converging principles "protect novelty" and "affirmative judgment" (Parnes, Noller & Biondi, 1977). Predecessor ALU (1985) built on PPC (1982). UALo puts even more weight on positives first.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.3.5, pp. 186-190. Starting point: 2 to 5 preselected options.

name: Making a Poster
diamondNote: Solution Finding
materials: Flip-over sheets, markers in different colours, masking tape
purpose:
Turns a fragile idea into a sturdier concept. The poster format makes the RG cover what Acceptance Finding will need (an inspiring name, an explanatory sketch, a short description), which forces them to define the idea and make choices. New questions and challenges usually surface along the way. The finished poster is a strong way to share understanding and start a conversation.

Use it to:
• Develop options further.
• Turn abstract ideas and discussion into concrete decisions and concepts.
• Prepare for Acceptance Finding.
inShort: Split the RG into pairs or trios. Each takes one or more converged options and combines them into a concept, presented on a poster using a format the facilitator provides.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Read the PaP aloud.
Set up the room. One table per subgroup, each with a flip-over sheet, A3 paper and black plus coloured markers.
Set the convergent mindset. Affirmative judgment: protect originality, trust the hedonic response, keep action in mind.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.
Form subgroups. The RG picks the options it wants to develop and splits into groups of two or three.
Make the posters. Hand out the format with the essential elements. Subgroups combine their options into one concept; about 20 minutes.
Check on progress. Walk around. If a group is stuck in discussion, suggest sketching on scrap paper first and simply starting. Give a five-minute warning.
Reflect. Sense readiness, especially the PO's, and energy.
Next step. Reverge by having subgroups present (e.g. Elevator Pitch), make more posters from other options, take a break, or set actions.

tipsAndTricks:
• The RG has usually already developed ideas in writing, sketches or talk before this.
• New questions will come up; have groups note them on a separate sheet.
• Sketching on scrap paper and a bit of time pressure help stuck groups.
• It isn't purely converging: making the poster swings between diverging and converging, and drawing it often triggers the next iteration.
• It can open up new opportunities, so ask groups to write down insights.
• Add an "origin" to the poster: which options it builds on, the motive, and the need, wish, issue or opportunity it answers.
• An energizer beforehand helps people get over a fear of drawing.
variants: • Early prototyping: build a 3D mock-up, prototype or experience instead, using clay, wood, Lego, paper or whatever's around. Acting out a service idea counts too.
background: The poster works as a "boundary object" (Star & Griesemer, 1989) that has to speak to different audiences. McWhinney (1992) describes four kinds of reality people construct: sensory, unitary, mythic and social. Tassoul (2009) turned these into a presentation checklist. The poster itself is the sensory part; it should also carry a description (unitary), an inspiring name (mythic) and what adopting it achieves (social). A sketch is essential. It's essentially a form of rapid prototyping.
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.3.6, pp. 192-195

name: Devil's and Angel's Advocates
diamondNote: Solution Finding
materials: Flip chart, markers
purpose:
A freshly made concept is fragile. The devil's advocate (DA) tests whether it can survive outside criticism and exposes weak spots worth working on. The angel's advocates (AA) build the case for it, equipping whoever will later champion the option inside the organisation.

Use it to:
• Find the weak spots of an idea, solution or concept.
• Generate ways to address those weak spots.
• Collect arguments for the option's benefits.
inShort: Start with 1 to 3 converged options. For the first option, one RG member acts as DA and the rest as AAs. After the pitch, the DA names weak spots, which go on a flip chart phrased as "How to…?" questions. The AAs respond, propose ways around the weak spots, and point out strengths, also captured. Repeat for each option with roles rotated.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Read the PaP on the wall aloud; the PO answers questions if needed.
Set the mood. The RG stands around the converged options with a flip chart and marker ready. Explain why Acceptance Finding matters.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.
Assign roles. One presenter pitches; one or two volunteers are DAs; everyone else is an AA.

Pitch and take notes. During the pitch, DAs note critical questions about difficulties, risks and points of caution. They're there to question, not to destroy the idea. AAs note benefits, unique aspects and success factors. Afterwards each side picks its top three.

Question and respond. A DA shares one critical question, which goes on the flip chart. AAs answer and build on each other; capture every defence. Repeat for questions two and three, then ask AAs for any positives not yet mentioned. Formally end the roles.
Reflect. Ask the PO whether the options cover the whole field and whether any area needs more exploration. Sense readiness and energy.

Next step. Repeat steps 4 to 6 for the next option with two new volunteer DAs. Then reverge on all questions and arguments (e.g. Idea Gallery) and agree actions for an action plan, have presenters develop the option further in pairs (e.g. Making a Poster), take a break, or wrap up.

tipsAndTricks:
• Use it carefully and on purpose.
• Make clear exactly when the DA role starts and stops; it isn't played outside that window.
• Timing is everything: too early and it kills creativity.
• Give the DA role to one person or a small subset, never the whole RG.
• People still find it annoying to have their idea challenged. Keep criticism on the option, never on people or their remarks.
• Remind DAs the goal is reducing uncertainty and risk, not killing the idea. It's about learning.
variants:
• Dominican Monks Exercise (Stortelder, Bijl & van der Vijver, 2011), for two people who disagree. They stand about three metres apart. A states their view, throws a ball to B and steps forward. B summarises until A feels understood, says what they agree and disagree with, then gives their own view, throws the ball back and steps forward. A does the same. The real difference in opinion surfaces fast.
• Six Thinking Hats (de Bono, 1985): a framework more than a technique. Black hat is the devil's advocate and yellow the angel's. The others are white (facts), red (feelings), green (alternatives) and blue (overview, keeping the goal in mind).
background: Irving Janis (1971) studied disasters like the Bay of Pigs (1961) and blamed "groupthink", the drive for consensus in cohesive groups. One of his nine remedies was to have at least one member play devil's advocate when alternatives are evaluated. The term comes from the Catholic Church's Promotor Fidei, whose job was to argue against candidates for sainthood (Fanning, 1911).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.4.1, pp. 198-201

name: Force Field Analysis
diamondNote: Solution Finding
materials: Flip chart, markers
purpose:
People who weren't in the session don't see why the output makes sense, and they have no emotional stake in it. FFA makes the RG aware of every force for and against the idea, and produces options that ease acceptance and implementation in the wider organisation.

Use it to:
• Strengthen ideas, solutions or concepts.
• Prepare to win acceptance outside the RG.
• Prepare an action plan.
• Identify stakeholders, both likely opponents and allies.
inShort: Pick one option to focus on. List as many driving forces (assistors) and restraining forces (resistors) as possible, assistors first. Prioritise both lists. Then generate ways to amplify the assistors, and ways to reduce, avoid, bypass or even reverse the resistors.

stepByStep.text: Focus. Read the PaP on the wall aloud; the PO answers questions.
Set the mood. Gather the RG at the flip chart and explain why Acceptance Finding matters.
Explain the technique. Purpose, outcome, steps.
Converge: pick an option. The PO chooses where to start. Describe the desired situation, e.g. the option implemented or developed further in the organisation.

Diverge: list forces. Assistors on the left: who'd support or help, what helps reach the goal, which resources are available. Then resistors on the right: who might oppose or hinder, what stands in the way, which resources are missing.

Reverge, then converge: prioritise. Discuss the forces with the RG (valid? can they be influenced? what if we do nothing? which are critical?) in a reverging mindset. The PO then ranks them, most critical on top.

Diverge: generate options. Start with the top assistor and ask how to strengthen it, recapping the diverging rules. Move to the top resistor and ask how to weaken, remove, overcome or flip it. Continue down the lists until the PO is satisfied or time is up.
Reverge: turn options into actions. Read the options per force and shape them into concrete actions (e.g. by when is this needed?).
Check on progress. Ask the PO whether the forces cover the field, whether the options push in the right direction, and whether they're the kind wanted.
Converge: pick high-impact actions. The PO circles the actions with the most impact.
Reflect. Run FFA on another option? Any area to explore further? Sense readiness and energy.
Next step. Another FFA, put the chosen actions in an action plan, or take a break.

tipsAndTricks:
• Put everything on Post-its so reverging is easier.
• Think broadly about influences: resources, affected business processes, attitudes of people and groups, parallel projects.
• Consider bringing in outsiders to name forces.
• Pushing harder breeds resistance, so spend enough energy on the resistors.
• Identify stakeholders upstream and downstream of the problem. Inviting them into the RG boosts acceptance a lot.
• Changing one force can shift others or create new ones.
• 5W1H helps find forces (who could help, what could benefit, where, when). Use Why to understand a force and build arguments, and How to start generating options.
• Managers like to score force strength for go/no-go decisions. The authors advise against it: the numbers are subjective and easy to manipulate.
variants:
• Assistors and Resistors (Isaksen et al., 2000): a similar technique under another name.
• Resistance matrix (Van Leeuwen & Terhürne, 2010), stakeholder-focused: options as rows, stakeholders as columns, each cell scored from ++ (active support) through 0 to −− (active resistance). Then generate ways to reduce resistance.
• FFA and Mind Map: put the idea at the centre of a mind map, branch out its first-order consequences, then second and third-order ones, positive and negative. Run FFA on those consequences. Similar to Glenn's (1972) Futures Wheel.
• Politics 101 (Segal, 2001): role-play the real stakeholders instead of devil and angel. List stakeholders and pick the key ones; each RG member plays one while another pitches the idea. Each stakeholder says what they'd gain, what they'd lose, and how the PO could win their support. One flip-chart sheet per stakeholder.
background: Kurt Lewin (1947, 1951) developed FFA for change management: think in terms of moving from the present level to the desired one rather than a fixed goal. Implementing a session's output means change, which Lewin framed as unfreeze, change, refreeze. FFA is a good way to prepare for the unfreezing. It's now common in organisational management (Schein, 1996; Thomas, 1985).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.4.2, pp. 202-207. Starting point: 1 to 10 options you'd like to take forward after the session.

name: Parking Lot
diamondNote: Any
materials: Flip-over and black marker
purpose:
A session runs on what's known beforehand and what's in the RG's heads. Information Finding is the link between the session and the research and development that follows. The Parking Lot handles that link.

Use it to:
• Let the RG raise any topic while the facilitator keeps control of the process.
• Connect the session to the follow-up work.
inShort: A simple way to keep the session on track. Concerns and questions that would otherwise block someone get acknowledged without derailing the task. Participants write them on Post-its and stick them under the [P] during breaks. A "To find out later" (TOFOL) section turns gaps in knowledge into follow-up work.

stepByStep.text: Set up. Prepare a flip-over sheet headed [P] with a "To find out later" section. Hang it where the RG can see it, near the agenda and session goal.
Explain it. [P] is for questions and concerns that stop people from taking part. TOFOL is for information the project needs but nobody has yet. Explain how both are handled and answer questions.
Deal with the topics. Handle [P] items straight after each break, before resuming the plan. Handle TOFOL items at the end as What (to find out), Who (will do it) and When (it'll be ready).

tipsAndTricks:
• Use a distinct colour (e.g. red Post-its) for concerns and questions.
• Mention the [P] only at the start and don't keep reminding people. Usually nothing ends up on it.
• [P] and TOFOL are easy to forget in a busy, time-pressed session, so make them part of your routine. The RG has to be able to trust that parked items will come back.
variants: • Wonder Wall: another name for the [P], since it holds what participants wonder about.
background: Treating Information Finding, Content Finding and Acceptance Finding as separate processes is fairly new (Buijs, Smulders & van der Meer, 2009), so there are few Information Finding techniques in CPS literature. Gordon (1961) paired short Synectics sessions with longer experiments to test solutions. The first good description of the Parking Lot comes from the Metaplan school (Schnelle, 1979).
source: Road Map for CPS Techniques (Heijne & van der Meer, 2019), §3.5.1, pp. 210-213

name: Mind Mapping
materials: One A2 or flip-over sheet, Post-its, black and coloured markers per participant, wall space, the PaG printed large
materialsNote: Wall space; an A2 sheet works instead of flip-over
purpose: Explores a vague term in the PaG by writing whatever it brings to mind, one word per Post-it, connected by lines — surfaces both what's written down (books, named techniques) and what only passes by example (a mindset, a way of working no book captures).
inShort: Write the vague term in the centre of a sheet. The RG adds words that come to mind, one per Post-it, each connected by a line to the word that triggered it.

stepByStep.text: (3 min) Focus the group on the task. Write the PaG large and visible. Ask the problem owner to explain it and give an example of what success looks like. Ask for the outcome, not a solution form, so one obvious answer doesn't anchor the RG. Problem owner answers the RG's questions.
(1 min) Set the group. The RG stands around the large sheet. Hand out Post-its and markers. If the RG has more than 5 people, split into groups of 3 to 5 and add debrief time.

(1 min) Lead the RG into the diverging mindset. Remind them of the ground rules: postpone judgment, quantity breeds quality, hitchhike, freewheel. If participants offer solutions, write each on a Post-it and park it at the side.

(1 min) Clarify the process: a mind map explores a word by writing whatever it makes you think of, one word per Post-it, connecting each new word with a line to the word that triggered it. Both book knowledge and unwritten/mindset knowledge count. Use colours and symbols. Draw no boxes.

(4 min) Start the mind map. Write the centre word large. Say "write each word that pops up and connect it." If it stalls on one category only, ask "what has someone shown you that is not in any book?" If it stalls entirely, ask "go one branch deeper" or "what else?"
During the map, check on progress. Watch for judging, full sentences and boxes. Ask for one word per Post-it and unique words over generic ones.
(2 min) Reflect. Put the map on the wall. Ask the problem owner: "does this cover the field you have in mind? Is there an area to explore further?" Sense the energy of the RG.

tipsAndTricks: Prompt the RG twice during the same map: once for what's written down (books, named techniques), once for what only passes by example (a teacher's mindset, the kind of thing no book captures). A short dry run before the session helps facilitators know how to prompt it.
source: Team-authored for the Creativity Guru (Case 2) session plan, Step 2. The centre word used in that session was "creativity knowledge" — swap it per case. This resolves the earlier source contradiction between the PRD's seed-list table (which wrongly attributed this to a Road Map book page) and its narrative text (which correctly called it the team's own custom technique).

name: Force Fitting and interactive brainsketching
materials: Paper, markers or pencils, the PaP written large for reference
purpose: Produces many rough visual ideas, each tied to the PaP through the excursion.
inShort: For each option harvested from the excursion, ask what it suggests for the PaP, list the connection, then draw a picture to visualise the answer.
tipsAndTricks: Pass drawings around and build on them. The Creativity Guru session ran this for 35 minutes directly after the excursion; the team considered and dropped MATEC as too complex for that case, and a mentor confirmed force fitting plus brainsketching as a good combination in its place.
source: Road Map §3.1.4, steps 7 to 9, plus brainsketching. The purpose/materials/tips above are this technique's real execution in the Creativity Guru (Case 2) session plan, not a book transcription.

name: C-Box
materials: A large C-box drawn on paper or a whiteboard, dot stickers, markers
materialsNote: C-box drawn large on paper or a whiteboard
purpose: Selects ideas worth building and worth trying, without losing a bold one.
inShort: Locate ideas in a C-box plotted on two axes, then select from the strongest quadrant.
tipsAndTricks: Axes are case-specific — the Creativity Guru session used value creation for students (benefit to creative growth, not money) against student engagement (how much students want to take part): a book chapter can be high value and low engagement, a cartoon the reverse, so look for ideas strong on both. A joker card or dot can protect one bold, low-scoring idea if the problem owner says they can make a crazy idea work themselves. Confirm the axes with the problem owner before the session — they follow the case, not a fixed book default.
source: Road Map §3.2, Creadox — the book's own numbered steps aren't transcribed. Axes and tips above are this technique's real execution in the Creativity Guru (Case 2) session plan (20 minutes), not a book transcription.

name: Ice breaker: throw the answer
diamondNote: Diverging, light — opens the session rather than working the PaP
materials: Paper balls, 4 labelled containers or a dartboard, cards with method descriptions and alternative names
materialsNote: A dartboard works instead of containers
purpose: Set the mood. Show the value of preserved knowledge and why passing it on matters.
inShort: Recognise creativity methods by description or alternative name, then reflect on what they gave you.

stepByStep.text: (2 min) Welcome the RG. State the case purpose first, e.g. "Tonight's case is how knowledge from creativity gurus reaches students. [Problem owner] holds a large collection of their books and materials and wants students to use them." Let the problem owner decide how to tell the backstory.

(5 min) Play 3 rounds, about 90 seconds each. Read the description of a method, or its alternative name from the book. Show 4 answer options. Each participant throws a paper ball into the container of their answer. Reveal the answer. Ask: have you used this, and what does it connect to?

(2 min) Reflect. Say: "you are on this course, and you use these methods, because gurus put them into books, courses and teachers. Today you took part in groups or facilitated with them." Ask: what would you have missed if nobody had preserved them?
(1 min) Move on: "so how do we keep this knowledge reaching students? First we look at what it is made of."

tipsAndTricks: Keep it quick and light, with no scores — the source of an idea doesn't matter, but the link between names and ideas does, since one idea travels under several names. Take the descriptions and alternative names from the book and check them before the session. Setup: place 4 containers labelled A to D a few steps away; with a dartboard, use darts and four zones, decided on the spot based on the venue.
source: Written by the team for the Creativity Guru (Case 2) session plan, Step 1.

name: Purge on the PaP
materials: Post-its, markers, the PaP written large
purpose: Clear the obvious answers, so a following excursion generates options beyond them.
inShort: Write down every option that already comes to mind for the PaP, one per Post-it, until the pace drops.
tipsAndTricks: Read a few aloud, no discussion. This empties the obvious so the excursion isn't spent regenerating it.
source: Road Map §3.1.4 — the purge sub-step of "Creative Confrontation, excursion and forced fit" (see that technique's inShort: "Purge, excursion, force fit"), run as its own timed row in the Creativity Guru (Case 2) session plan rather than folded into one combined block. The book's own numbered steps for this sub-step aren't transcribed — the fields above come from that session plan, not a verbatim book transcription.

name: Generate How-To's and the PaP
diamondNote: Diverges into How-To's per cluster, then converges them into one PaP checked against SPARK
materials: Fresh Post-its, markers, a large sheet or wall space for the PaP
materialsNote: Or wall space for the PaP
purpose: Turns clustered output into a set of How-To's, then one PaP checked against SPARK.
inShort: For each cluster, write "How to convey [cluster] to students?" questions. Then choose and reformulate into one PaP.

stepByStep.text: (1 min) Explain: for each cluster, write "how to convey [cluster] to students?" questions, one per Post-it.

(6 min) The RG writes in silence and sticks each How-To beside its cluster. Split the time across the clusters and rotate. Default: many clusters, many How-To's, to diverge as much as possible. With few, similar clusters, write How-To's only for the most outstanding ones.
(3 min) Share the set of How-To's. Check whether each cluster opens a different solution field.

(5 min) Choose and reformulate into the PaP together. The facilitator writes, the RG edits. Check against SPARK: specific, positive, ambitious, relevant, keep it simple. The problem owner confirms the PaP is relevant. Read it aloud and write it large.

tipsAndTricks: If the RG stalls after 3 minutes, offer one of the prepared fallback PaPs.
source: Team-authored for the Creativity Guru (Case 2) session plan, Step 4. The SPARK check is the course's own PaP-quality concept (see the course vault's "Problem Statement (PaG and PaP)" note).

name: Wrap up
diamondNote: Closing activity, outside the diamond's three phases
materials: None. Keep the PaP, C-box and chosen idea visible on the wall.
materialsNote: Keep the PaP, C-box and chosen idea visible on the wall.
purpose: Close the session and agree the follow-up.
inShort: Thank the RG. The problem owner reacts. Agree what the client receives afterward.
tipsAndTricks: The client report needs this agreement up front.
source: Team-authored for the Creativity Guru (Case 2) session plan, Wrap up row.

name: Reflection: What? So What? Now What?
diamondNote: Closing reflection, outside the diamond's three phases
materials: Paper or notecards, pens
purpose: Participants name what they learned.
inShort: Each participant answers What? So What? Now What? alone, then shares.
tipsAndTricks: Ask the problem owner to reflect too.
source: IDEM104 course reflection model (see the course vault's "Reflection Model - What So What Now What" note). Used as the closing technique in the Creativity Guru (Case 2) session plan.
